House went into Committee of the Whole to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend * the Civil Service Act ' by providing for the employment in the office of the Auditor General, for a period not exceeding two years, of such temporary clerks as may be necessary in connection with the audit and payment of fees and expenses under the Dominion Elections Act.-Mr. White (Leeds).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE.
speechtext: I am not sure that any explanation is required in connection with this resolution. Action is made necessary by a difficulty experienced by the Auditor General, because of the amendment to the Civil Service Act. Prior to 1908, temporary clerks could be appointed by order in council for a period not exceeding six months, and the appointments could be renewed for six-monthly periods indefinitely. But under the amended Act, these temporary clerks can hold office for only six months in any fiscal year. Very heavy duties devolve upon the Auditor General in auditing the election accounts, and six months is altogether too brief a period for the proper performance of these duties. The work is such that trained temporary clerks are necessary. As the law now stands, the Auditor General trains clerks for a period of a month or so, and about the time they reach their maximum of usefulness he is obliged to dispense with their services. He advises me that he discussed- this matter with the leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), when leader of the government. That being so, I assume that there is no objection to the passing of this amendment. The Auditor General has only twenty of these clerks, but they are trained; and after six months the number will diminish. From the investigation I have made I believe that, if not absolutely necessary, at least it is highly desirable that this amendment should be made in order that the Auditor General may efficiently perform this part of his duty. I have figures here showing the amount of work, and other documents bearing on the subject, but I think it is not necessary to present them unless objection is taken.

Mr. COCHRANE moved the second reading of Bill (No. 77) to encourage and assist the improvement of highways.

Before we proceed to the consideration of this Bill I will have to ask your ruling on the ob-115
jection I raise that the Bill is not in order. It contravenes article 54 of the British North America Act, and rule 77 of our own rules, inasmuch as it is a money Bill to all intents and purposes. I have to call your attention to section 3 of the Bid which is in these terms:
The Governor in Council may, in any year, and upon such terms and subject to such conditions as are prescribed by order in council, grant to any province in aid of the improv-ment of existing highways or the construction of new highways in such province, or for both such purposes, a subsidy not exceeding such sum as may in such year be voted by parliament for that purpose."
The only answer which can be made to the objection I now raise is that the Bill does not actually dispose of money. The money which it is intended to dispose of in this Bill is to be appropriated later on; the appropriation is to be carried out later on. But the purposes for which the -appropriation is -made are now disclosed. I have also to call your attention to article 54 of the British North America Act, which makes my point very clear, that this Bill cannot be considered at this stage. In article 54 I find these words:
-It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address, or Bill for the appropriation of any part of this public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that House by message of the Governor General in the session jin which such vote, resolution, address or Bill is proposed.
I call your attention to these words:
To any purpose that has not been first recommended to that House by message of the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address or Bill is proposed.
The purpose now indicated in the Bill is the disposition of money which it is proposed to vote later on. But according to my reading of article 54, that very purpose must first be preceded by a recommendation to the House by message of the Governor General. Later on it is indicated that an appropriation will be asked for from parliament for a certain purpose, that is to say, to aid in the building of highways. But that purpose, according to my reading of section 54, must be first considered by resolution upon a message from the Governor General. As I said a moment ago, the only question which can be Taised is as to whether there is an actual disposition of money and I have to call your attention to the fact that according to the jurisprudence of the House upon section 54 the rule applies not only to moneys which are actually voted but to all Bills which involve an expenditure of money. You will find the explanation and authority in ' Bourinot,' page 568:



The constitutional provision which regulates the procedure of the Canadian House of Commons in this respect applies not only to motions directly proposing a grant of publio money, but also to those which involve such a grant.
Well, Sir, this rule applies particularly to this case. It is quite true that the Bill at the present time does not actually propose a grant of money, but it involves such a grant of money, because it is intended to make disposition of the money which it is proposed to ask for later on. Bourinot goes on to say:
A member who has not received the permission of the Crown has noti been allowed to move the House into committee on a. resolution providing for the purchase and exportation by the government of certain depreciated silver coinage.
Then he goes on to give another illustration of it, and I would call your particular attention to this:
In 1871 it was proposed to go into committee on an address to the Queen for a change in the Union Act, so as to assign the debt of old Canada to the Dominion entirely, and to compensate Nova Scotia and Now Brunswick in connection therewith; the Speaker expressed the opinion adverse to the proposal on the ground that it was intended as preliminary to legislation imposing a public burthen, and was consequently not a mere abstract resolution which did not necessarily involve a future grant.
This decision of Mr. Speaker Cockburn is to be found in a book which we have in the library entitled ' Decisions of the Speakers of the Legislative Assembly and House of Commons of Canada,' No. 181. On the 6th March, 1871, Mr. Dorion moved as follows:
That this House will, on Wednesday next, resolve itself into a committee to consider the following resolutions:-
1st. That the division between the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec, of the surplus of the debt of the former province of Canada, over and above the sum of $62,500,000, assigned to the Dominion of Canada by the British North America Act, presents great difficulties, which it has not hitherto been possible to overcome in a satisfactory manner.
2nd. That the difficulties, resulting as well from the uncertainty as to the amount of the debt to be divided, as from the absence of an acceptable base for the making of such division, and that of the assets remaining in common to those two provinces, threaten to give rise to serious embarrassment.
3rd. That for the avoidance of such difficulties, the debt of the former province of Canada should be assigned entirely to the Dominion, as though it had been so from the first, with compensation to the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia for the share which those provinces would have to pay upon the surplus of that debt.
<iir WILFRID LAURIER.
4th. That an humble address be presented to Her Majesty, praying Her to be pleased to recommend that the British North America Act, should be amended in accordance with
these resolutions.
There was no disposition of actual money in that resolution; it was simply that an address be presented to Her Majesty praying for an amendment to the Act so that
the parliament of Canada could make a disposition of money as between these different provinces. Objection was taken by Six George Cartier:
That the resolution cannot, under the provisions of the 54th section of the British North America Act, 1867, be considered by the House, unless recommended by message from the Crown.
Mr. Speaker decided as follows:
The motion proposes that an address he presented to Her Majesty, praying Her to recommend that the British North America Act be amended, so that the public debt of the Dominion be increased, and that compensation be made to the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
In my opinion this motion cannot be entertained, it being in contravention of the 54th section of the Imperial Act for the Union of British North America. In that section it is provided that this House shall_ not adopt any vote, resolution, address, or Bill, for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, &c., &c., to any purpose that has not been first recommended by message of the Governor General. The contention

On the part of the mover, presumably,
-is that the proposed appropriation being beyond the power of the parliament of Canada, this provision of the statute cannot therefore apply.
If any answer is made to my objection this will be the answer:
The contention is, that the proposed appropriation being beyond the power of the parliament of Canada, this provision in the statute cannot therefore apply.
Mr. Speaker Cockburn went on as follows:
In its literal construction it does apply to the motion, and certainly it seems to me to the full as necessary in a constitutional sense, to interpose the check of a message from His Excellency, under the responsibility of his ministerial advisers, before adopting an address which may be followed by legislation, imposing a burthen on the people by a parliament and ministers, owing it no responsibility, as in the case of a Bill or motion for the appropriation of money within our direct control.
The same question came before the House again a few days after in a different form. Mr. Dorion again brought the matter to the attention of the House, by moving as follows:

That an humble address be presented to Her Majesty, representing that an equitable and satisfactory division of the surplus debt of the late province of Canada, between the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, is not likely to be effected in the manner provided by the British North America Act, 1867, and that the difficulties which beset the question have been greatly aggravated by the award rendered by the arbitrators appointed by the Dominion government and by the government of Ontario, in the absence of any arbitrator for the province of Quebec, which is regarded by the government and the people of Quebec as illegal and unjust, and praying that Her Majesty be pleased to recommend the passing of an Act by the imperial parliament, so amending the British North America Act as to authorize the parliament of Canada to deal by legislative enactment with all questions connected with the said surplus debt.
That was simply an abstract question, and it was met by Sir George Cartier with the following amendment:
That all the words after ' that in the original motion, be left out, and the following inserted instead thereof:-' The validity of the award rendered by the arbitrators appointed by the Dominion government and by the government of Ontario in the absence of any arbitrator for the province of Quebec, being contested by the province of Quebec; and the government of Canada having come to the conclusion not to act on such award until its validity shall have been determined by a competent judicial tribunal, this House refrains from expressing an opinion on the award so rendered.
Mr. Chaveau moved in amendment to the amendment that:
It 19 highly desirable that the difficulty now existing between the provinces of Quebec and Ontario concerning the divisions and adjustments of the debentures, liabilities, credits, properties and assets of Upper and Lower Canada, provided for by the British North America Act, be speedily set at rest, and that this House will give its most favourable consideration to any measure to be introduced by the government, having this object in view, and involving any aid on the part of the Dominion commensurate with the importance of the object itself, and with our resources; due regard being had to the rights of the other provinces.
I would specially call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the effect of this amendment:
That this House will give its most favourable consideration to any measure to be introduced by the government, having this object in view, and involving any aid on the part of the Dominion commensurate with the importance of the object itself, and with our resources.
There was nothing there to bind the House. It was simply a proposition that this House would give its most favourable consideration to the object which would 1154
be a charge upon the public revenue. Objection wa3 taken by Mr. Mills and the objection was sustained. That was on the 9th of March. On the 13th of March, Mr. Speaker Cockburn made the following statement to the House:
I observe that it is entered on the Journal of the 9th March, that upon objection taken by the honourable member for Bothwell, the motion of the honourable member for Quebec county was declared out of order for the reason there alleged.
I desire to correct that entry. The motion was out of order, in my opinion, not because it proposed an appropriation of public money, within the meaning of the 54th section of the British North America Act, and should have been preceded by message, but because it involved an increase of the public debt, and should, therefore, have been first considered in Committee of the Whole.
I am aware that it is doubted whether it is a correct rule of parliamentary practice, that every abstract proposition which, if acted on, would increase the public debt of the country, should be first considered in committee, but my opinion on the point has been expressed on two or three occasions, and I shall so continue to decide, unless the House should think proper to express a contrary opinion. This rule, however, being self-imposed, may be enforced or relaxed, as the House shall determine. But the constitutional rule, contained in the 54th section of the Imperial Act, is one that, being absolutely binding, should be neither extended nor restrained by implication but should, at all times, be most guardedly considered by the House. I desire, therefore, to correct the error on the ' Journal ', so that the precedent shall not be understood as having any relation to the 54th clause of the Constitutional Act, 1867.
What is most remarkable about this, is that the opinion of Mr. Speaker Cockburn on that occasion was ordered to be printed in the Journals of the House, and it was, therefore, incorporated as a rule of the House, which has not since been repealed, and which is at present the law of this House. In my humble opinion, the case seems clear that the present Bill, although it does not actually appropriate money, is the first step towards the appropriation of money, involving therefore, the appropriation of money and is consequently quite within the rule as interpreted by the Speakers who have been your predecessors in office, Sir. I have only to add that this objection is not made in any captious spirit, but it has a purpose behind it, and a very important one. The Bill that is now before us, proposes a wide departure from what has been hitherto our constitutional law. It proposes to extend to the build-ins of new roads or the improvement of old roads, moneys out of the federal treasury, and which roads have hitherto been under the charge of the respective provinces. I do not say that I am against this legislation; on the contrary, I think, under

the circumstances of our buoyant revenue, this legislation ma-v be wise, but we have certainly the right to take exception to the manner in which it is proposed. It proposes to give to the Governor in Council all moneys that may be appropriated, without any regard to the future action of parliament, and to bind ourselves in advance without any rule to be followed, but simply the intention or the action of the government of the day. If we are to discuss this Bill, and vote appropriations of this kind, the time when we should dispose of the manner in which the money is to be expended, is when the money is appropriated, and therefore, it should be first of all, introduced by resolution, when any objections which may properly be urged against the legislation .should be urged. All the conditions which are to be attached to the expenditure of that money, should be set forth- at the time the principle of the Bill is being discussed. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I invite your ruling upon the objection I have raised, for the reasons I have given.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We have no fault whatever to find with the right hon. gentleman for raising the question which is always an important one to consider in connection with the introduction of Bills. The very language of the British North America Act, which he has read, shows that there is no ground whatever for the objection my right hon. friend has made. Section 54 of the British North America Act reads :-
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or Bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or .impost to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that House by message of the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address, or Bill is proposed.
I venture to submit that this Bill is not within the meaning of that section. It does not appropriate any part of the public revenue, it does not appropriate one dollar of the public revenue for any such purpose. It merely does this: It provides that if parliament shall at any future time appropriate a certain sum of money for that particular purpose, then that money shall be expended by the Governor General in Council under the provisions of this Bill, according to the method now laid down in the Bill before the House. The provisions of the Bill are perfectly simple and plain and not to be misunderstood.
The Governor General in Council may in any year and upon such terms and subject to such conditions as are prescribed by order in council grant to any province in aid of improvement of existing highways or the construction of new highways in such province, or for both such purposes, a subsidy

not exceeding such sum as may in each year be voted by parliament for that purpose.
Therefore, it is apparent that before one dollar of public money can be expended under the provisions of this Bill, a resolution must be brought down in parliament, assented to by His Royal Highness the Governor General, considered in Committee of the Whole, and be the foundation of a Bill which will alone justify any expenditure under this Act. When I have said that, it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that I have said all that is necessary to be said upon this subject. Not one dollar can be expended under this Bill until a resolution has been brought down in the House of Commons, passed through Committee of the Whole, and until it has also passed through all the stages of a money Bill in this House and in the Senate. Therefore, to suggest, as the right hon. gentleman has done, that this is a Bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenues, seems to me to be entirely a misstatement of the case. The simple answer to it is, that without this Bill, if an appropriation were presented to this House, passed through Committee of the Whole and embodied in an Act of this parliament, the Governor General in Council would be left without any machinery whatever for the expenditure of that money. This Bill is solely designed to furnish machinery for the expenditure of a certain sum of money which may or may not be voted by parliament for that purpose. There is no question of the appropriation of one dollar of the public revenue of this country for this purpose until an appropriation Bill has been brought in founded upon a resolution which shall conform to section 54 of the British North America Act.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:
There is nothing more to be said on this point, and I shall now proceed to the consideration of the Bill itself. We had an explanation of this measure on the first reading. The Bill is a short one, and, as my hon. friend himself stated in introducing it, is rather meagre. It disposes, in a manner which I think it not in accordance with true constitutional principles, of the money to be expended, by giving the control of it absolutely to the Governor in Council without any guidance as to the manner in which the expenditure should be made. The Bill contains only six clauses. The first is the title. The second is the definition of the word 'Minister'. The third provides:
The Governor in Council may, in any year, and upon such terms and subject to such conditions as are prescribed by order in council, grant to an^ province in aid of the improvement of existing highways, or the construction of new highways in such province, or for both such purposes, a subsidy not exceeding such sum as may in such year he voted by parliament for that purpose.
The fourth section provides simply that the specifications for the improvement and construction of highways are to be contained in an agreement between the minister and the government of the province, and are to be approved by the Governor in Council before the money is expended. The fifth section provides:
Each highway to be constructed or improved shall be defined or described in such agreement, and provision may be made therein for the future _ maintenance of such highway in good condition according to a specified standard and to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council.
These are all the dispositions of the Bill. Under this Bill, if it were to pass as it
is, the Governor in Council would be given the most extraordinary powers. We on this side of the House have no exception to take to this new departure for the purpose of aiding in the construction of highways out of the federal treasury. This has not been the practice hitherto, but in the affluent condition of the treasury today, it may not perhaps be unwise that we should apply money in that direction. Moreover, the demand for highways is today more acute than it ever was before, and if it is intended to build new highways, of a certain standard and to assist the various provinces in that respect, for my part I see no objection. The only exception I have to take to this Bill is that any such exception should be made upon some rule provided for in the Bill, and should not be left to the whim or caprice or favour of the government of the day. If this Bill passes in its present form, any appropriations for this purpose can be devoted to one or two or three provinces, according as the ministry of the day may determine, In a matter of this kind there should be a principle of equity and equality applied as between provinces. What is to be the line that is to determine how the money shall be expended? Shall the larger provinces of Ontario and Quebec be taxed for the benefit of the smaller provinces, or shall the new and younger provinces be taxed to enrich the already richer provinces? Shall the whole matter be left to the ministry of the day without any rule of guidance? I think hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House will recognize that the Bill in its present shape is altogether undesirable and goes to the verge of un-[DOT]con stitutilon ality if it be not altogether unconstitutional. I submit that any expenditure of this kind should be regulated by some principle. Now, what shall that principle be? For my part, I submit that the only principle for the expenditure of such money is the principle to be found in the British North America Act, which in section 118 provides that the moneys paid out of the treasurv to the various provinces shall be according to population. This provision was amended subsequently, complaint having been made that the allowances to the provinces were based simply upon the census of 1861. There were several conferences of the provinces, first in Quebec and then in Ottawa, commencing in 1887, all protesting that the allowances made to the provinces were not made on the principle of population, but on the population as it was in 1861.
It was felt and contended with great force that the allowance should be regulated on the principle of population, not on the fixed population of 1861, but on the moving population as determined by each census. There were several conferences of the provinces, they all joined


unanimously in asking that the principle should be amended so that the allowance should be made on the scale of moving population as determined by each census, In 1907 this House unanimously adopted this view, amended article 118, and provided that thenceforward the allowances to the provinces out of the treasury should be in accordance with the population as determined by each census. This seemed to me the most regular and the fairer way of approaching the subject. I do not presume that any man in this House will find fault with me if I say that there should be some principle to regulate these appropriations and I do not believe that any fairer principle can be found than that of population. If any-think fairer can be devised I would be willing to consider it, but after giving the matter the best consideration I could, I did not find anything fairer than the principle of population. The great province of Ontario would be the largest beneficiary out of this appropriation. Nobody can find fault with that because if the province of Ontario is the wealthiest of the provinces it is also the province which has the largest charges to maintain. The province of Quebec would come next. This would also be natural because the province of Quebec has also large charges on her treasury. Therefore, I submit that this House should adopt the basis of population in making these grants and that the appropriation should not be left to the arbitrary disposition of those who for the time being happen to be the advisers of the Crown. Therefore, I beg to move:
That the Bill be not now read, but that it be resolved that while the House is favourable to the granting of federal assistance towards the construction of permanent roads it is of opinion that such aid should be given to the governments of the provinces for such purposes, aud should he granted on a fixed basis similar to that now prescribed by the British North America Act and amendments thereto for subsidies to the provinces.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister).
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) professes warm sympathy with the purposes of this Bill, but he adopts a very peculiar way of indicating it. He meets the Bill with an objection which was made at the first reading and answered at the time. Unless his memory is very short indeed he did know that the question as to the allotment of any moneys to he voted by parliament was raised on the first reading of the Bill by himself and an answer was given at that time by the minister in charge of the Bill, the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane), Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
who said that the distribution of this money among the different provinces was to be on the basis of population or to use the phrase he then used: On the same basis as that on which the subsidies are granted to the provinces. My right hon. friend seems to have doubt on that question now, notwithstanding that assurance. Let me say to him that that doubt is unnecessary.
This is not a government which proposes to deal upon the principle of warm sympathy and cold justice, which actuated hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. When these subsidies are brought down we propose to vote a specific amount for each province which cannot be appropriated to any other province, and we propose to proceed on the basis of population or amount of subsidy. So. far as I understand, that will amount to the same thing. My right hon. friend also says that this Bill gives extraordinary powers to the Governor General in Council. In that he is mistaken again. This Bill was introduced by my hon. friend, the Minister of Railways and Canals, who in framing it, adopted the analogy of at least half-a-dozen Acts introduced by the right hon. gentleman or his government. I refer to the Bills providing for railway subsidies. It is impossible in a Bill of this kind to indicate particular highways, because the province in each instance must be consulted in regard to that. Provision is made for consultation and co-operation with them. But apart from that, the sale-guards which have been introduced in this Bill by the Minister of Railways and Canals, with regard to the character of the highway, and the expenditures of this money upon permanent work and upon work that will bring the highway up to a particular standard, have all ibeen taken from the Bills providing for subsidies to railways, and according to the very lines of these measures which have been introduced not only 'by the late administration, but by previous administrations.
I do not know that there is very much else in what my right hon. friend has said that deserves consideration. I do not propose to reserve to the Governor General in Council, power to determine what amount shall go to one province or another. When the estimates which are necessary before one dollar can be paid over in aid of the construction or improvement of a highway are introduced it will be found that they provide for a particular amount to each province and that those amounts will be regulated according to the principle mentioned by the Minister of Railways when he introduced the Bill.
My right hon. friend speaks of the importance of highways. They are very important indeed, and it is for that reason that this proposal has been made in order that

provinces with limited revenues may thus he enabled to keep up the standard of their highways, and that that standard may be improved from time to time, by means of this grant from the federal exchequer of Canada. I think that is a very worthy purpose.
I do not claim that this Bill is a perfect Bill. It has been prepared in the hurry of a session, by a government which had to meet parliament within five weeks after it assumed office, and the Minister of Bail-ways and Canals, who introduced the measure, stated that it was introduced as the best method of dealing with this matter that could be devised by the.government in the short time at their disposal for its consideration. It is very likely that in the next, or the following session, a more elaborate measure may be introduced, but it is considered desirable by the government that no time should be lost in implementing the pledge made by the Liberal-Conservative party in the last elections, that it would provide aid from the federal treasury of Canada towards the improvement of highways throughout the country.
I have not found that this proposal has been greeted by the people of Canada in quite the same spirit as that in which the right hon. gentleman seems to regard it. I have found unanimous approval among the people towards a measure of this kind, which follows the analogy of the Eailway Subsidies Act, reserving to the Governor General in Council, certain control over the expenditure, in order to ensure that that expenditure may be made wisely and in the public interest.
We have no desire or intention to discriminate against any province on the ground of the political complexion of the government; we propose to deal with every province justly and fairly and without the slightest discrimination. We shall be glad indeed, after the close of this session, to take up this matter with the governments of the nine provinces of Canada, and to deal with them on fair, reasonable, and just lines, in order that this expenditure may be wisely and properly made. Having regard to these considerations, it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that there is no ground whatever for the obstructive motion which the right hon. -gentleman has made, which seeks to delay the passing of this measure, and to prevent the people and governments of the nine provinces of Canada from receiving any measure of assistance_ from the federal treasury for the very important purpose of improving the public highways. I should have thought that if my right hon. friend had entertained the opinion that the principle of this Bill was in the public interest, he would have allowed the second reading to pass without seeking to delay or obstruct it, and would have
sought to introduce by way of amendment., to the Bill in committee, some of those precautions which he mistakenly supposes to be necessary in regard to the measure. He has not seen fit to take that course. He has asked this parliament to postpone the second reading of this Bill to another day, and to pass a resolution which is entirely unnecessary in view of the statement made by my hon. friend the Minister of Eailways and Canals, on the introduction of this Bill. The resolution says :-
That this House is of opinion that such aids, should be given to the governments of the provinces.
The third clause of the Bill does that very thing:-
3. The Governor in Council may, in any year, and upon suc-h terms and subject to such conditions as are proscribed by order in council, grant to -any province in aid of the improvement of existing highways or the construction of new highways in such province, or for both such purposes, a subsidy not exceeding such sum as may in such year be voted by parliament for that purpose.
It is perfectly true that section 6 makes another provision
6. The minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council and uopn such terms and conditions as are prescribed by order in council, may undertake the construction of any new highways or the improvement of any existing highways in any province, and may expend in such improvement or construction the whole or any part of the sums voted by parliament for such -subsidy to that province. Provided, however, that the minister shall first obtain the necesary authority from the legislature of such province and the consent of the Lieutenant Governor in Council.
Thus, not one dollar can be expended under section 6 of this Act without the authority of the provincial legislature, and the consent of the provincial government having been first obtained. So that this is a Bill to grant aid to the provinces- in-the first instance, under proper regulation by the Governor in Council, in order that the money may not be expended for any other purpose and may not be unwiselv expended, or else it provides an expenditure by this government in any province but only with the consent of the provincial legislature, but also of the provincial government. Are not the rights of all the provinces, and all the provincial governments thoroughly safeguarded under the proposal? The right hon. gentleman's resolution says also:-*	.
The assistance should he granted on a fixed basis similar to that prescribed by the British North America Act and amendments thereto.
He was assured on the first reading of the Bill, and has been assured again today, that when the estimate in furtherance of the purpose of this Bill is introduced

into this parliament, the amount payable to each province will be set forth and that amount will be based in each instance, upon the population of the province, and upon the subsidies founded upon that population. Under these circumstances, it does not seem necessary for me to say anything further in reply to the observations of the right hon. gentleman, but to ask this House to vote down his proposal and let us proceed with this Bill in order that the highways in the nine provinces of Canada may be improved by means of aids from the federal treasury with the least possible delay.

It does not need the statement of my right hon. friend the leader of the government, that this Bill was prepared in a hurry to convince members of this House of that fact, for an examination of the Bill, I think, will show them that the measure is of the most slip-shod character, that it is rough, crude and immature in its structure. And, having in view the importance of the subject, I think it would be difficult for any hon. member to call to mind any Bill introduced into this parliament which has shown such a want of care in preparation. I do not wonder that my right hon. friend the leader of the government thought it desirable to make the excuse which he has made. But he coolly tells us that if the time be given, if we will leave it with the government until another session comes round, having more leisure,, they will no doubt prepare a measure which will be more acceptable to parliament. That is the effect of what he says. He says that the government have not had very much time to prepare a measure. Well, they have been in office since the 10th of October. From current rumour, they have been very busy, but only in one direction-in wielding the axe, and decapitating officials in the public service, and have not even had time, some of them to give attention to the business of their departments. After four months we have a Bill which takes up not quite two pages, and which certainly could not have occupied a great deal of time. And I do not think it would take a great deal of time to prepare a Bill which would be thorough in its character, and would accomplish what is intended. There was a rumour that the Bill was hurriedly prepared, and submitted to parliament in order to give some evidence to one constituency in Canada-the constituency of South Renfrew-that the government intended to improve the highways. For the report in the public press shows that very great stress has been laid upon that provision, and very great efforts made to capture votes in the constituency by reason Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
of the government having determined upon this policy.
So much for the reason of the hurry: which the right hon. gentleman admitted in connection with the preparation of this Bill. Now, he admits that the Bill ought to contain the provision embodied in the amendment of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition.
He did not say so.

He admits, in effect, that the moneys ought to be expended upon that basis. If that is so, I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the members of this House, that before we are called upon to support this measure these provisions should be in the Bill. The Bill is of the most meagre description, as I have said. It contains no statement as to the basis to be adopted for the expenditure of these moneys.
It lays down no principle upon which the government shall act. All we have is the statement of my right hon. friend that when, later on, they come to submit estimates to parliament, they: will ask for amounts for the different provinces. If that is the intention of the Bill it ought to say so. Before parliament is to be committed to this expenditure there ought to be a provision as to what shall be the basis of the appropriation. Now let me call your attention to the third section of the Bill:
The Governor in Council may, in any year, and upon such terms and subject to such conditions as are prescribed by order in council, grant to any province in aid of the improvement of existing highways or the construction of new highways in such province, or for both such purposes, a subsidy not exceeding such sum as may in such year be voted by parliament foT that purpose.
Under that section it would be open to the government to come down to parliament and ask for a total vote for the improvement of highways throughout Canada, and if parliament passes this Bill with that section, we shall entrust to the Governor in Council the manner in which this lump sum shall be divided between the different provinces. If my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, when he had this Bill drafted, had clearly fixed in his mind that there should be a definite sum for each province to be voted by parliament, based upon population, I think he would have said so in the Bill, I think he would have laid down distinctly the basis upon which the appropriation should be made. Either he had not made up his mind when the Bill was drafted, or had not time to prepare a section which would cover the ground when the Bill was submitted to parliament.
Now as to section 4, I think it is a very wise provision that a highway which

is to be aided shall be built or improved, as the case may be, according to descriptions, provisions and specifications approved by the Governor in Council on the report of the minister. I think it is very desirable, and everybody will admit it is desirable, that federal aid should Only be given to what,, as stated in the amendment of my right hon. friend, may well be termed permanent highways. There should be no federal aid given to roads of a temporary character. The highways which the federal government are to aid ought to be in the nature of main highways,- of important highways, and those highways should be built up to a high standard, and be in all respects permanent roads.
I object to the Bill upon another ground, that it leaves it open to the government to take either one of two courses. They may either make grants to the provinces in aid of the construction of highways and allow the moneys to be expended by the provinces, or they may make arrangement for the construction of some highways as federal works entirely, and entirely outside co-operation with the provinces. I think we ought to determine upon one course or the other. Either these grants for permanent highways should be entirely for the provinces, and we should allow the provincial governments to expend the moneys, subject to the specifications being approved by the Minister of Railways, or we should, as a federal government, undertake the construction of these permanent highways ourselves. We should not have an alternative provision in the Bill. That I think is a most objectionable feature of it. I think hon. gentlemen on consideration will see that it is objectionable. See what an opportunity for undue influence it gives to the government of the day in respect of any province. If they cannot agree as to the specifications with regard to any particular highway, or as to the particular highways to be aided, then the Minister of Railways can very well say: Oh, well, we will undertake the construction of highways in some particular province where we don't want the provincial government to have anything to do with the matter; we will undertake the construction of those highways ourselves. It is true, the right hon. gentleman says that the government cannot do that unless with the approval of the government of the province. But you can easily see what an engine for pressure upon the government of any particular province this would give to the federal government of the day, in case this section were passed. Surely there can be no objection, if these grants are to be based upon the population of the province, to limiting the provisions of the Bill to that mode of aiding public highways. I think it is extremely objectionable that this doublef-barrelled provision should be contained in the Bill, that in some provinces, or in some localities in a province, the provincial government may have charge of the building of highways; and in other provinces, or in other portions of the same province, the federal government may carry on the construction of a highway as a federal work. I think heretofore highways have been entirely attended to by provincial governments and by the municipal authorities, largely in co-operation with the provincial governments, and I think the better way would be that, whatever money the federal government is to give towards improving or constructing highways, should be handed over to the provincial authorities. Then there is another objection which I find in section 6. Certain roads may be undertaken as federal works.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Only with the consent of the provinces.

That is objectionable, because if that is done, you may have to have a staff of highway engineers in the employ of the federal government to carry on these federal works. I submit it should be one way or the other; either the federal government should take charge of the highways-which, of course, would be limited to trunk lines or main highways -and aid "this work entirely as a federal work, to which a strong objection can be urged, or the work should be done wholly by the provincial governments by means of the money which is to be paid out by the Minister of Railways. I think myself the proper way is to leave the matter of expenditure to the provincial governments, always making provision that the highway to be aided is subject to the approval of the minister.
Now I think there is another provision which ought to be in the Bill. It ought to be provided that if, during any year, a provincial government does not expend upon highways the amount to which they would be entitled according to population, that money should remain in the federal treasury, and should bear interest, to be paid over to the provincial government at such date as it will be required for the particular highway it was proposed to undertake; that is to say, that if the amount is not expended in any one year, the province should not lose it, but it should remain in the fund to be added to the payments which might subsequently be made.
Now in conclusion, I think my right hon. friend the leader of the government is not doing himself the greatest possible credit when he accuses the leader of the opposition of obstructing this Bill. I see no obstruction to the Bill. My right hon. friend

the leader of the opposition is simply moving an amendment declaring the opinion of this House that the Bill ought to contain just what the Prime Minister I think himself is almost disposed to admit, and which he would have inserted in the Bill when it was brought down if he had given the subject longer consideration. All that the leader of the opposition is contending for is that a principle should be adopted that the whole people will approve of. If the leader of the government were to approve of the suggestions contained in this amendment* it would be the easiest thing in the world to adopt the amendment, take the second reading of the Bill to-day, and then we could expedite it in every possible way. There is no disposition on this side to obstruct the Bill, We are anxious to facilitate its passage just as much as gentlemen on the other side of the House, but what we do desire is that when this Bill passes it shall be a proper Bill, that when this parliament engages to approve of the appropriation of federal moneys for the construction of highways, the Bill shall provide that the appropriation shall be based upon the proper principle. We say that the principle should be the population of the different provinces which is the basis upon which the subsidies are now payable under the British North America Act. With these objectionable features removed, and the Bill improved and made what, I am sure, my right hon. friend the leader of the House will agree the Bill ought to be, because he says that is the way in which they propose to work it out, he will find no disposition upon this side of the House to offer the slightest objection but every disposition to facilitate its passage just as rapidly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to congratulate the government and the country upon the introduction of this Bill. I can hardly conceive of any Bill which would be more to the credit of the government, or which would give more substantial benefit to the country than this Bill. I congratulate the country particularly because it is a distinct act in favour of the farmer and the rural population. With a somewhat lavish hand, at all events with very great generosity, we have been from year to year voting large sums of money for the construction of railways, the development of our canal systems and the improvement of our ocean ports, but we have not been doing very much that brings aid directly to the farmers' door. For many years I have felt that, however much we might devote to the construction of railways, so long as the main highways of the country remain in the imperfect condition in which they have existed in Canada, the farmer will be handicapped both as regards Mr. PTJGSLEY.
getting his products to the markets of the world and also in the matter of the valuation of his land. There is nothing which detracts so much from the ready sale of land at a good price to people coming from Great Britain visiting Canada and inspecting our homesteads as the fact that they contrast the condition of our roads most unfavourably with that of the roads they have been accustomed to in the land they come from.	*	_
So, I hope that the government, having embarked upon this policy, will be generous-very generous indeed, almost lavish- in the expenditure of money which will so directly concern the farmers of Canada.
I congratulate the government, too, upon the fact, which seems to irritate and annoy hon. gentlemen oposite, that the government have not lagged back and for years and years been prodded on to implement their promises, but that they have come down at the very first opportunity to make good the promises which were made on the hustings or elsewhere in this regard. It does not agree with our hon. friends opposite, because they are not accustomed to that kind of thing. It does not agree with them for another reason- because they know that it is in such marked contrast with the flagrant way in which they disregarded their^ promises during the whole period of their administration, and so the people cannot be slow to notice the contrast between the present administration and the administration recently led by the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). So. this government have brought down this measure speedily, in haste, in a hurry-as the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Pugsley) says, bearing evidence of hurry-and to the extent to which it may bear evidence of hurry it redounds all the more to the credit and honesty of the present administration, as showing that they are prepared to-day, tomorrow, and always to advance step_ by step in the redemption of the promises made on the hustings and otherwise to the people of Canada. So, I hope it will always be. These hon. gentlemen do not understand it. For sixteen years they avoided the fulfilment of every promise-I think every promise-they had ever made. I think I have heard them say tha,t they redeemed one, but I do not know which one it was. I could never recognize any.
The reform of the Senate was one.

The manner of my hon. friend from Simeoe (Mr. Lennox) is so different from the benevolent and smiling addresses which he used to direct towards us in opposition, that I cannot help thinking that he is sharing in an unusual degree the evidence of perturbation and excitement which are animating the ranks of our opponents generally today. Recent events have evidently produced an undue effect upon my hon. friend from Simeoe. I am surprised, very much surprised, at the tone and substance of the remarks of the Prime Minister. He terms this amendment an obstructive amendment. I think he cuts the feet from beneath such a charge by the admission which he himself made that the Bill was drawn up in a hurry and was capable of improvement, and, if the Bill be capable of improvement, what more natural on the paTt of the opposition than immediately to attempt to improve it. Sir, this is not an obstructive amendment; it is an improving amendment. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister's argument faltered

so and his manner was so different from usual that I could not fail to recall a few nights ago our having the assurance of so high an authority as the Minister of Trade and Commerce that if a certain event happened yesterday it meant the injection of venom into the veins of the government. Most clearly the venom is in the veins of the government and a double portion of it appears to be in the veins of the Prime Minister. We on this side of the House hope it will go on working, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce prophesied it would work, until the government is destroyed. Now, the amendment proposes to insert in the Bill a provision that this expenditure upon the highways shall take place upon a fixed basis. Of course, if we were always to have in power a Minister of Railways such as the present, I do not ' know that such an amendment would he necessary to be written in the Bill. We know that he is a non-political minister; we who have listened to him in the House are aware of the almost metaphysical detachment of his intellect. We know the high planes of political thought in which he wanders-; he takes no interest in elections; elections are things apart altogether from his consideration. We know his political career; he would never use the money for highways for the -sake of winning an election; no one could think it for a moment. But, then the present Minister of Railways will not always be in power. We have the assurance of the Prime Minister, and I accept it, that he would not use this money for such a purpose and that so far as his government is concerned this money for roads would never be used for electioneering and poli-cal purposes. The fact that my right hon. friend gave us that assurance almost amounted to an admission that as the Bill is drawn it suggests that that is a possibility, because the suggestion did not proceed, so far as I heard, from the right hon. the leader of the opposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon, it was in reply, to a remark made by the leader of the opposition that I spoke.

I may not have heard the address of my right hon. leader as carefully as did the Prime Minister who was to reply, and therefore I accept the correction. In any case I accept the statement of the Prime Minister that he himself would be the last man to use this money in such a way. But I contend that the force with which he made the denial indicates the suspicion that the way this Bill is drawn up would leave such a possibility open. I say to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister as I said in regard to my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, that he will not be in power Mr. CLARK (Red Deer).
for ever. Recent events would almost indicate that he may be in power for only a very short time. From all that I hear by correspondence from every portion of Canada, his government has gotten in wrong, and there is widespread thought in the minds of the people of this Dominion, and in many cases in the minds of people who are not by any means strong Grits, that this will be a short lived administration.
Hear, hear.
Oh.
Be that as it may, I am going to take a ground that gentlemen opposite -cannot jeer at, and I say: you wont' be in power for all eternity.
Hear, hear.
And, it may just be that when this government-to which I will attribute for the moment all the perfections that they themselves claim-passes out of power, some wicked Grit administration may come in.
Never.

Well, there is a gentleman over there who believes in eternal possibilities. As I say. some wicked Grit government may come in which would use this Bill improperly. Why not provide against such a possibility in the future; why not act in some reasonable and statesmanlike manner in respect to this matter. There is a better reason to demand that the government should accept this amendment and that is, because the Prime Minister only differs by a hairs-breadth from the leader of the opposition. He tells us that the government purposes doing what the amendment demands they shall write it down they will do. His purpose is exactly the purpose of the amendment only that the government prefers to keep a loose hand; they prefer to keep a roving commission.
If the principle be a good one-and every man of us, on both sides, I think, will be inclined to follow our respective leaders in agreeing to the principle-none of us dare do anything else in the face of public opinion-if the principle be a good one, why not put it in the Bill? What has the hon. gentleman to fear about printing it? If the Bill has been drawn in a hurry, we have at any rate taken enough leisure to arrive at the common opinion that the object is a good one. Then print it in the Bill, and it will bind not only this administration], but future administrations* as well.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend who has just sat down has put the issue very properly to the leader of the government. The leader

of the government told us that his Minister of Railways and Canals, in moving the first reading of this Bill, stated that this money was to be paid to the provincial governments that was the purpose and object of it.
No. I was asked by the right hon. leader of the opposition on what basis the money was going to be expended, and I said on the same basis on which the subsidies were paid.
That means exactly what I said, that the provincial governments were to receive this money in the same proportion in which the subsidies are at present divided.
No.

If that is not the
meaning of the Minister of Railways, I am at a loss to know what the English language means.
Read ' Hansard,' and you will find.

Perhaps my hon. friend will explain; I do not want to take any advantage of him. I understood the right hon. leader of the government to say that the Minister of Railways had taken that position in moving the first reading of (the Bill, and he himself stated to-day that the object was to utilize the money provided under this Bill in the same way as the subsidies to the provinces were granted. That being so, my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), has put the proposition to the House in a form from which there can be no escape. If that be so, there can be no objection to the Premier causing to be put in the Bill that provision in the amplest and clearest way. That is what the leader of the opposition seeks for in his amendment. It is absolutely essential, it seems to me, when you come to consider this whole question, apart from the abstract way in which my hon. friend from Simcoe put it, unless by some unseen method the federal government of Canada shall provide money for the highways. Underneath this proposition is involved the question of the relative powers of the provinces, and the Dominion in regard to the building of roads. Now, under the British North America Act the sole right to deal with local works of that character is vested in the provinces. Outside of the western provinces, where the title to the land is still vested in the Dominion, the title to all the highways is vested in the provincial governments or in the municipalities, as the case may be.
In the west also.

That being,so, the federal government, for the first time in
the history of confederation, are proposing to step within the boundaries of provincial authority and legislate on this matter. Now, why was this question of roads left to the provincial governments? Why have the provincial governments been needing more money in order to deal with them properly? Why was the suggestion made that 'the federal government should provide funds for this purpose? Simply and solely because apparently there has not been enough money in the hands of the various provinces to deal with the highways as 'the public opinion of the country would [DOT]like them to be dealt with. In order that the provincial governments might be in a position to deal wtih the highways and other matters, the federal government in 1867 agreed to give certain amounts by way of subsidies to the provincial governments to be expended by them for this and other purposes within their jurisdiction. That was the reason why, from that period down to the present, the federal government has granted subsidies to the various provinces. The area within which the provincial governments could raise money by taxation was defined and circumscribed in such a way that it was impossible for them to obtain within that area the necessary money which would enable them to keep pace with the development of the provinces. As a consequence, there were repeated conferences of representatives of all the provincial governments, in which the whole question of the relation of the subsidies to their expenditures was discussed, in 1887, in 1902, and in 1907, when the provincial premiers met and decided to ask the Dominion government for larger subsidies in order that the needs of the various provinces might be properly supplied. The result was that in 1907, the federal parliament gave to the provinces increased subsidies. All the while the provinces have been dealing with 'the question of roads. In the province of Ontario at confederation there was vested in the municipalities the right to deal with this whole question, and the municipalities have gone on raising money by direct taxation for the purpose of improving the roads. I understand that the same system obtains in Quebec. The governments of these two provinces have used provincial funds for the purpose of building colonization roads. In the province of Prince Edward Island there is no municipal government, but the provincial government has maintained the whole road system of the province out of the subsidy paid by this government. In the province of Nova Scotia we have never had munci-pal taxation for roads except that there is vested in each municipality the right to tax up to a certain amount each year for the purpose of improving the roads, but

the title to the highways is vested in the province, and the provincial government makes expenditures in various parts of the province for the improvements of the roads. The same principle prevails in the province of New Brunswick. Where does the money come from? From the subsidies paid by this government under the terms of 1907. That is the position of affairs. Some of the provinces repair the roads, and there are municipal road inspectors, whose salaries are a matter of criticism in some 'quarters on the ground that a certain amount of money is voted for that purpose.
Then you come into another arena and you have a provincial road inspector and his staff of assistants whose salaries and expenditures are also deducted from the total amount provided by the central authority and you have criticism there as to the large amount that is expended. Does the right hon. the Prime Minister propose under this Bill to set up a third system of officials in Canada to deal with the question of roads or does he not? If he does we are going to have a very peculiar condition of affairs. You will have municipal officials paid out of municipal funds, provincial cfficials, responsible to the provincial government but really paid out of the funds of this government and then federal officials paid out of the money provided for in this Bill. Roads have been discussed 'in my province for years and the leader of the local Conservative party has been preaching there during the last four or five years that the one thing wanted in regard to road expenditure was unification of authority, the adopting of a more comprehensive plan to which every one would give adherence.
This is not a subject which can be treated lightly and my right hon. friend cannot dispose of the proposition of my leader by speaking of it as obstruction. I am sure the right hon. leader of the House will realize the position of affairs that for the first time since 1867 the federal parliament is entering upon this arena which is peculiar to provincial governments and that in so doing he is interfering with provincial rights. True you may be interfering in a way which the province will not mind, you are going to give them money but you are entering upon the trend of an expenditure which is wholly confined to the provinces, you are undertaking to go in and spend money on roads which has never been done before. It will not do for my right hon. friend to say that this resolution follows in a general way legislation used in regard to subsidies for railways. It is all very well to reserve to the Minister of Railways and his engineers the right to prescribe the methods and the usual restrictions under which subsidies can be earned by the construction of rail-Mr. MACDONALD.
ways. That involves only the making of certain specifications well known to engineers, But here we have a new departure. The government say to the minister: you are going to start out for the first time in the history of confederation on a Bill made in a hurry without deliberation, without stating in the document the thing' you say you are going to do. No one has a right to enter upon a constitutional question in such a light hearted and careless way as these hon. gentlemen are doing.
Are you against the Bill?

I am in favour of the federal government giving to each province by way of additional subsidy more money for the improvement of roads. That is my position and I hope it is my hon. friend's because I understood the Premier t0 say that was his position and all we want to do is to put into the Bill a statement of the fact, a statement of the position of the Premier. Of course the Premier says that this money which is to be expended under the first five sections of the Bill has to be spent in co-operation with the provinces. It is true that you have to deal with the provinces. Why does not my right hon. friend amend that a little and say that the sums of money to be granted shall be in proportion to the amounts which have already been granted to the _ provinces by way of provincial subsidy? My right hon. friend goes further and by section 6 of the Bill proposes a system of expenditure which is not by way of subsidies to the provinces. That is a peculiar clause of the Bill, an entirely new proposition, and one which calls for the fullest consideration by this House. He tells us theTe is not much to be criticised about that because if the federal government propose to go in and expend! money itself in any province, it cannot enter upon the expenditure without obtaining the necessary authority from the legislature of the province. Of course it cannot, how could it? The title to the highways is vested in each one of the provinces. It is very doubtful if there is any necessity for the latter portion of the provision. What power or authority has this government to interfere with the roads in any province of the Dominion? These roads are held by the Crown in the right of the province, not in the right of this Dominion. My right hon. friend would be a trespasser, and any one of his officials would be a trespasser if he went on any public highway without the consent of the provincial government concerned. Not a dollar could be spent for that purpose except with the consent of the provincial government. If that is so would my right hon. friend tell us whether the government intend to inaugur-

ate a new department to be known as the department of highways, as stated in the newspapers, [DOT] through which department the minister is going to start upon a system by which the federal government will deal with the highways of the country? The right hon. gentleman tells us that is not the policy of the government. If that is the policy of the government we want to know, because if so, this parliament is entering upon an absolute interference with provincial rights, and undertaking to deal with matters over which they have no jurisdiction, and with which they cannot deal except with the concurrence of the provinces.
What objection would you have in the case of an interprovincial road?

My hon. friend would have to come before this House! with a separate proposition dealing with that problem, and it would require the greatest possible care. Of course, we have Section 92 of the British North America Act, which gives to the legislatures the Wght to deal with local and private works "within a province, except in respect of such works as may be declared for the general advantage of Canada, but the use of highways in that connection up to this moment has never formed the subject of consideration by this parliament. Of course the federal government has legislated in regard to railways which were interprovincial works, and I have heard hon. gentlemen opposite wail on this question of provincial rights in the last parliament and before the Railway Committee, day after day, complaining about the federal government undertaking to grant local charters.
As they had a right to do.

Then they ought to be thinking about provincial rights in connection with this Bill. This House| has not yet secured from the government a statement as to what its policy will be. In replying to the right hon. leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), the right hon. the leader of the House (Mr. Borden), said that the Bill in the pre-i amble states that this money is to be spent on the same basis as the provincial subsidies. My right hon. friend is going to carry out_ that policy. Let us go on in the enacting clause and provide for that assistance. But the nigger on the fence is this section 6, and it is in regard to that that I hope the Minister of Railways, when he comes to speak, will tell us whether or not it is the purpose of this government, over and above the assistance they propose to give by way of subsidies, to inaugurate a new department to be known as the department of highways, withi officials and all that. If that is the proposition I submit to the House that before we consider it, the government 'ought to place before the House a Veil defined plan dealing with the various conflicting bodies that have to do with road expenditures in this country to-day.
The unification of authority and expenditure is the policy of the Conservative party in the province of Nova Scotia, in provincial affairs. Is it the policy of the leader of that party in federal affairs ? That is the question upon which we ought to be informed. Have the government had any inquiries made on this subject throughout the country ? The Prime Minister is reported to have said to a deputation that waited upon him about two weeks ago that it was not the intention of the government to engage in the repair of old roads, but to engage in the construction of new ones. If that is so, we ought to know it; if it is not so, we ought to know that. I saw that statement'reported the other day; I do not know whether the Prime Minister cares to give assent to it now

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am responsible for what I said, not for what is reported.
Sotne hon. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

That is, of course, not a very brilliant remark. But it does not take much to please our friends opposite since the event of yesterday. But perhaps they should rather wait for some greater utterance on the part of their leader before they break forth in applause, for, certainly, that remark of his was not exactly profound. He is responsible, of course, for what he says, aud not for what he is reported to have said. Well, that only means that the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane), when he speaks, will have to tell us a little more fully what is the policy of the government in this regard. Either the policy of the government is to construct new roads or its policy is to repair old ones. This discussion, I am sure, has shown, it must have satisfied hon. members, that there are very great questions involved in this Bill which cannot be disposed of so easily as is suggested. Has the Minister of Railways made any inquiries whatever with regard to the conditions under which this federal money is to be granted ? For, unquestionably, section 6 provides for the granting of that money. Has the minister any information and comprehensive plans to submit to tbe House ? If he has not, then the House ought not to give adherence to a Bill that is put forward apparently on the basis that the *money is to go to the provinces, yet with a little clause behind to enable some kind

of system to be built up foT other reasons. Clearly we are entering upon an arena of legislation for the first time since 1867. This means that we ought to take great care in framing that legislation. The Prime Minister's statement that the Bill was prepared in a hurry and perhaps is not so complete as it might be, but a better one, a wider one, will be introduced at another session, is not good enough for this House. Legislation under which it is proposed to trespass upon provincial authority ought to proceed with the greatest deliberation and oare, and before we are asked to crystallize this Bill into law we should understand thoroughly what we are doing. Each and every one of the provinces of the Dominion, at a conference or in some other way, ought to be consulted upon the question how far they are willing to give up their authority in relation to highways and the expenditure on them, before such a measure is introduced. It does seem to me that, so far as federal assistance to highways is concerned, us the leader of the opposition proposes, it should be confined to grants based upon the provincial subsidies.

So far as I could follow the hon. member for Pictou, (Mr. Macdonald), his chief objection seemed to be that the Bill involved a new departure. A strange doctrine, surely, to come from a so-called Liberal in this House-that,, because this is without precedent, because never before in the history of Canada, has a government been in a position, and been wise enough, and broad enough, to introduce a measure such as this for the benefit of the people of Canada, therefore the measure is to be declared bad. This is a measure for the benefit of all the people, irrespective of class, or occupation or of where they live; it applies to every province and covers the whole Dominion.
I have also been amused by the attitude of our friends on the other side, with regard to an occurrence of yesterday. One does now begin to realize the depth of gloom into which these gentlemen were plunged, when one finds them rejoicing with exceeding great joy-over what? Over the fact that they have been able to hold half the majority they had on September 21. Just as proper would it be for our friends the Dutch, to rejoice over taking Holland, or the Irish over the retention of Cork, as for these gentlemen to rejoice so hugely because genial George, the Bill Nye of Canadian politics, has been able to hold South Renfrew, by something like half the majority by which it was carried on the 21st of September. Why do not these gentlemen remember, do they not realize, that the ' great chieftain ' was there with his ' white plume.'? How could George help Mr. MACDONALD.
being elected under the circumstances. True, the ' white plume ' did not have much effect on the 21st of September, but it did seem to be able to hold what they had on the 22nd of February.
Now, my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), finds fault with this Bill, because it is crude, rough, rude. He is such a polished, courteous gentleman, that I can understand how his sensitive soul would be affected by anything that is rude. He also complains of the Bill because it does not go enough into detail. He has forgotten the investigation of the Central railway. If he had remembered that, he would not have spoken against this Bill, on the ground that it did not contain details enough. He will remember that there was a Bill referred to there; it was brought up in the evidence,-a Bill in which was so little detail that it had on it only ' Five thousand W. P.' So, surely the hon. gentleman was not serious when he spoke of this Bill as being improperly drawn because it did not go sufficiently into detail.
It seems to me that the people of this country will look with very little favour upon the criticism of .hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to this matter, whether that criticism be based, like that of the hon. member for Pictou, on the lack of precedent for the introduction of a measure of this kind, or whether it be criticism like that of the hon. member for St. John, based on the statement that the measure is crudely drawn and the language not so perfect and not so Addisonian as if it had been drawn by the hon. gentleman himself. I think the people of this country, irrespective of party, will hail this Bill with great satisfaction, implementing as it does, the promise of the party now in power when it went to the country in the late election, and showing that this government is a government which proposes to carry out the pledges it made to the people, in sharp contradistinction to the party that, for the last fifteen years, misgoverned this country, who carried out no pledges that they made. They said they did carry out their pledges with regard to the Senate, but it was Providence that helped them out with the Senate and ' reformed ' that body to the extent to which it was reformed by making the majority Liberal instead of Conservative.

I do not intend to detain the House more than a few moments. But this question of good roads is one which, in the section of the province of Ontario from which I come, is of such momentous importance, that I feel that it is my duty to say at least a few words in regard to the Bill before the vote is taken on the amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

I might say without, perhaps, wounding the feelings of the hon. gentlemen, that if they have, no better arguments to advance in favour of this Bill than those put up by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, they have a very weak case. Now, if it were not for the last clause in this Bill, I would not care much whether the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition were carried or not. But it seems to me that clause goes to the very crux of the whole matter. The right hon. leader of the government has told us that the Bill was quickly drawn, perhaps crudely drawn, and will be supplemented perhaps by a better one during the recess. We wish to supplement it by a better one now, and to define clearly and emphatically how the distribution of the money shall be made so that there may be no dispute about it hereafter. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has very properly stated that though the right hon. gentleman is Premier at present, he might not be Premier next year, not that his party will be defeated, but that he himself, whom we hope will live long, might not be in this House. There are lots of contingencies that may arise between' now and the next session of parliament, and another leader, another king, may arise who knows not Joseph ; another king may arise who may not feel that he is "bound by the statements of the present right hon.
