Prime Minister of Canada, and who may not agree that this money should be divided in accordance with the suggestions made to-day by the leader of the government. So that, now is the accepted time, now is the time to rectify this Bill, and put it in the exact shape in which the leader of the government says he intends to put it. There is no question of obstruction. The amendment can be adopted now and the Bill can be put through probably this afternoon or at the beginning of next week. I want it to be distinctly understood that I am not endeavouring to obstruct the passage of this Bill. I am strongly in favour of this government granting aid for the construction of good roads throughout the country, and will do everything in my power to assist the passage of a Bill for that purpose. But I desire to protest against the way this money is to be expended. Though it may aid in the construction of good roads throughout the country, it can also be used in a way which will not conduce to the advantage of the people, or to the construction of these roads in such a way as we would like. I have my own views as to how this rtfoney should be distributed, and those views I intend to suggest when we are in committee on this Bill. I am not in favour of handing this money over to the provincial legislatures at all, but of paying it 116
out to the municipalities directly, as the provincial governments do-of course under certain restrictions and with certain supervision. That is the proposition which I believe the people of the province of Ontario would approve. I think it would meet with the approval of ninety-nine per cent of all the municipalities in the province, that the money should be paid directly to the counties and not be paid to the provincial government. If the municipalities did not use it properly, then let this government implement, or supplement, whichever word you like to use, the moneys paid by the provincial government in that direction.

I agree with the right hon. the Prime Minister that, judging by the remarks we have heard from hon. gentlemen opposite, their idea is to obstruct tnis Bill. As I understand parliamentary procedure, the discussion that takes place on the second reading is for or against the pnnciple of the Bill, and hon. gentlemen have been talking directly against it. Now 1 clo not know of any other federal government which has adopted this system of aid-!ng . gnways, that work has generally been left in charge of the provinces. I do not know of any other country where the federal government contributes or co-operates with the province for that purpose, as it is proposed to do in this Bill. At Washington, I understand, there is a Bureau of Education for the very purpose of instruct-lng the people on the necessity of good highways, and the manner of constructing them I think probably it would be well if we had in Canada such a bureau as that because the construction and upkeep of public roads are certainly very necessary in a country like ours. I want to correct a statement made by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) in his reference to what I said on the first reading of this Bill. The right hon. the leader of the on-position asked me:	1
I would ask the hon. gentleman to tell us it there is any basis of allotment among the provinces. The provincial subsidies are based based on population?

It is to be on the same basis as that on which subsidies are granted to the provinces, in other words, by population.
I have no doubt whatever but that this government can work in conjunction and in harmony with the provincial governments in carrying out the purposes of this Bill. I think every provincial government, whether Grit or Tory, will welcome this Bill and co-operate with us in carrying it out. Moreover, the government will not undertake to force any local government to join us if they do not wish to. I hope we shall be able to arrange with the provincial governments so that they will



make a grant equal to the grant given by the federal government, and that we may be able to go on within a very short time and construct these roads. But if any provincial government does not wish to contribute, I see no reason why we should not go on and do the work ourselves. But if they join in with us, so much the better. We will, co-operate with them in making the specifications. Evidently no specifications can be laid down in this Bill. You cannot draw up specifications to cover all roads, because some might cost much more, and others much less than others. The right hon. the leader of the opposition objected to putting so much money in the hands of the Lieutenant Governor in Coun

cii. What did they do last session, or the session before? They gave a subsidy to a road to be built from Montreal to join the Transcontinental railway in Quebec, and there was no company named to which the grant was to be made; it was left to the government to name the company, and they manipulated it in such a manner as to give the money to their friends. We do not propose to take that course; we propose to work with the provincial governments, not with individuals or with companies. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I beg to move the second reading of the Bill.
Amendment (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) negatived.
Motion (Mr. Cochrane) agreed to, Bill read the second time and House went into committee thereon.
On section 3-grant of annual subsidy for highways.

I would like to ask my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) if he would explain what he has in his mind as being the purpose of these words:
The Governor in Council may, in any year, and upon such terms and subject to such conditions as are prescribed by order in council.
I would understand that terms and conditions would have reference to the specification of the roadway.

I thought so at first but on reading the section which comes next I have my doubts because the next section provides exactly for the specifications:
i. Any highway for which aid is granted to a province shall be improved or constructed, as the case may be, according to descriptions, conditions and specifications approved by the Governor in Council on the report of the minister, and specified in each case in an agreement between the minister and the government of the province, which agreement the minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council, is hereby empowered to make.

,
I think this clause is perfectly unobjectionable; on the contrary, quite proper, but it disposes of the specification in so far as clause 3 is concerned. My hon. friend must have something else in his mind. I do not exactly understand what the purport of those words is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There are a great many considerations which will occur to my right hon. friend in addition to_ those already mentioned. It will be desirable, for example, to have precaution taken that the money should be expended for this purpose and this purpose alone.

That is hardly what is meant. The money must be expended for this purpose; it cannot be expended for any other. I ask for this information because I have been unable to satisfy myself as to what is intended. I do not see what conditions are to be imposed which are not to oe found in section 4.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: I have no exception to take_ to the statement which my right hon. friend has made; there must be conditions which will be covered by the agreement, but everything that has been said by imy right hon. friend so far comes within and is covered by section 4. It is because section 4 is there that I do not appreciate the purpose of the words ' Upon such terms and subject to such conditions,' which are to be found in section 3; I would again call my right hon. friend's attention to section 4.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is entirely as to the character of the road.

No, that covers everything. Section 4, as I understand it, means that money may only be given to the province after an agreement has been made in regard to the specification and the conditions and everything else about the road. Then, I ask what is the meaning of these words in section 3?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
Are not all of
these comprised in the section?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. I believe ' the descriptions, conditions, and specifications,' refer only to the character of the road, and the expression in section 3 deals with matters to which I have alluded, and many others that I might suggest. It is impossible to foresee at the moment what terms and conditions may be thought desirable, but, those conditions I have brought to the attention of my right hon. friend will no doubt occur to him as- conditions that ought to be agreed upon between the governments before the money is handed over.
I do not dispute that at all. I simply say that in my humble opinion that is included in section 4.

I call the attention oi tire Minister of Railways and Canals and of the Prime Minister to my suggestion that the best way to distribute this money and the proper policy to adopt is, not to pay the money directly to the provinces, but to distribute the money among the various municipalities in the same manner as the Ontario Act distributes the money among the municipalities in Ontario. The Minister of Railways knows that the Ontario legislature -appropriated $1,000,000 in aid of good_ roads in that province, and that money is distributed by granting to each municipality one-third of the -money which that municipality itself 'expended for the 'construction of good roads.
It is given to the county -municipality.

That policy has worked out with the greatest possible degree of satisfaction and that is the policy which I am convinced ninety-nine per cent of the county municipalities in Ontario would wish to see adopted with reference to this money. In this way you will do away with all possible chances of extra officials. You can say to each county municipality: When you have expended $20,000 or $100,000 in the construction of good roads according to certain specifications and standards, we will pay you a proportion of the money you have expended. If you give the money directly to the provinces it simply means an increase of the provincial subsidy because the province is very likely to use this money for good roads, but they will not use any money of their own for such a purpose.

What the hon. member (Mr. German) says may sound very plausible, but you have to consider how it will work ouit. Should the Dominion government take upon itself the burden of direct-

ly dealing with all the county municipalities in Canada? I do not think so. This emphasizes just the meaning of section 3 as contrasted with section 4. The right lion, the leader of the opposition will not think it is an unfriendly statement if I say that lie has told us a great many times that lie is not a business man and I think that is true of him so far as I have been able to observe from his actions. There is a very clear emphatic distinction between clauses 3 and 4. Clause 4 is directed to the character of the road that shall be 'constructed and in which the Dominion government will put its money, but it goes no further, while clause 3 deals with the question of the terms upon which the Dominion will agree to give its money. For example, some o'f the municipalities have adopted toll gates upon their highways and the Dominion government would probably say: As we are expending this money not for local or sectional purposes but for the general advantage of Canada, we insist that the beneficial results of this work . shall not be hampered in any way by the erection of toll gates, and if you have toll gates we will not pay over any of this money. It may be true that this money could be best expended through the instrumentality of the county councils. The government of Ontario arranges that by contributing a certain proportion of the amount expended by the municipalities upon the improvement of the highway. We might make it a condition, if we wished to, that this money shall be expended directly through the county councils in certain cases where that system has been found to be working satisfactorily, and we might say: We will pay the money over to the province to be handed by the province to the county municipalities. It might be that in the case of a very expensive bridge we would contribute a certain amount towards it if the province would contribute another certain amount.	[DOT]

Will the hon. gentleman approve of the proposition, as far at any rate as the province of Ontario is concerned, that the money should be expended by the county councils in the same manner as the appropriation of the Ontario legislature ?

No, I do not say that I would go that far, though the system has worked fairly well. The Dominion parliament, in dealing with this matter, can, if it chooses, stipulate that the money shall be expended by the municipalities in such a way as tlhe hon. gentleman refers to.

On section 3, grant of annual subsidy for highways,

I think the importance of this legislation justifies the new departure. Perhaps it has scarcely dawned on the people of this country what this measure means to the rural sections of Canada, and to the agricultural interests. Let us look at what has been done elsewhere in regard to highways. In France, for instance, a country where agriculture has reached as high a condition, perhaps, as in any country in the world, they have 23,600 imiies of what tare called national highways, 28,600 .miles of departmental highways-all of these roads being paid for by the state-390,000 miles of municipl roads, upon which there is an annual outlay of 125,000,000 francs, or $25,000,000, and, in addition, a great mileage of what are known as rural roads, narrow roads connecting with the greater highways throughout the country. Consider also what is being done in the United States. In the state of New York, a few years ago, they bonded the state to the extent of $50,000,000 for the purpose of improving the roads, and the state proposes to build absolutely at the public expense 3,000 miles of state roads. They propose also, with the money raised by this issue of bonds, to assist what they call towns-we call them townships. In the state of Ohio, the estimate generally accepted is that the improvement of the road system adopted by the state, has increased farm values by from 25 to 50 per cent.

I asked the state engineer of what is called the State Commission, what effect the improvement of roads in the state of Massachussets had had in bringing back occupants to the abandoned farms, of which they have a good many, and he said that hundreds had returned to the farm in consequence of good roads. So it is a very important matter from that point of view. I am glad to see the unanimity existing in the House with regard to the importance of this question.
Now, it might be wise to consider carefully whether we should not have, to some extent, what we might call federal loads built and maintained by the federal authorities. There is danger, if you come down to the municipalities with this money, that we will have a lack of uniformity, we will not have that distinctive system which should govern the outlays on these roads. Now, we have nad some experience in Ontario with reference to giving municipalities money for this purpose. Several years ago there was what is known in Ontario as the Municipal Loan Fund. A number of counties borrowed largely from this fund, while others did not borrow from it. Some counties borrowed so largely that, after a few years, they found it difficult to pay; and away back in 1871 or 1872, I think the Hon. E. B. Woods devised a scheme of settling this vexed question. The legislature passed a law to forgive the debt to many of the borrowers, and in order to do justice to those who had not borrowed, they gave them so much per head. Now, it was not easy for some years to see any real benefit following the gift of that money to the municipalities. The difficulty was that they lowered their taxation instead of using the money to make improvements. I suppose under this Bill that difficultly could scarcely occur, because this money cannot be put to any other purpose than that of assisting in road construction. But. if you relieve the people along the line where you build one of these roads from road taxation, then there should be some arrangement by which the province would tax them for the purpose of forming a road fund, to build roads some where else. There has been a good deal said with reference to some definite plan or scheme being mentioned in the Bill. If you consider for a moment the varied climate of our extended country, you cannot have any uniform system that would apply to all the provinces, because our winter in some parts of the country affects the roads adversely. If you go into the far west and into British Columbia where they have a mild winter a different system would apply altogether. Then another thing is that the material out of which you have to build roads is of a
different kind in different sections of the country. There are some places where road material is much more easily got than in other places. All these matters have to be considered in dealing with this question.
The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), has raised the question of provincial rights. I think there is very little danger of any sharp trouble arising on this point so long as we are giving them something. The difficulty under the administration 'the hon. gentleman supported, was that the government was always taking something away from the provinces. That was a very different proposition. I am not a lawyer, but I believe this question of provincial rights, is largely a growth of sentiment rather than a difficulty in law. Expediency must to a large extent decide these questions between the federal and provincial authorities. Now the Americans are strong on state rights. When the federal government in the United States proposed to appropriate large sums of money to lend to the state for the purpose of encouraging agriculture, they said in the Act by which they made the appropriation that nothing in this Act should interfere with the right of the state to deal with this question; and there was no difficulty. Now it seems to me there ought to be no difficulty in this country, because our system is more elastic than theirs. I do not fear any difficulty along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Pictou. It seems to be that it will be ultimately a matter of agreement largely between the provinces, and the federal authorities. I think the direction of the road, or the location of the road, will largely be decided by conference between the provinces and the federal authority, because you must of necessity consult the provinces in a matter in which they have to so large an extent the local control.
Now, I feel that it would not be an unwise thing for the federal government to build certain roads as distinctively federal roads, and maintain them as such, because the question of maintenance is as important as the question of construction, and perhaps more so. If a road is not properly maintained, then you might just as well not build it, because it will very soon become dilapidated and useless. That is the experience of every one. Now, I wish to say that so far as I am concerned the proposal of the government has my most hearty and warm support. It is something that will affect the future of this country as nothing else will do that has been proposed for a number of years. As has been so well said by hon. members on both sides of the House, if we make such large outlays in other directions affecting trans-

portation, the burden of which has been largely thrown upon the agriculturalists throughout the country, and white he ha(3 to bear his share of other burdens in which he is also interested, the time has come to consider the advisability and wisdom of doing something to help the farmer, to get nearer to the door of the man who has worked so hard to solve the agricultural problems of this country. I can see no reason why this scheme should .not be carried out successfully, and in such a manner as to result in general welfare to the country. I was much interested in reading the early history of the eastern New England States in reference to roads. Before the railway, there was a strife between different neighbourhoods to secure what was then known as the ' general travel ' along those roads. The well-to-do people who rode in their carriages would choose the best roads, and the different farming communities vied with each other in constructing good roads so as to secure that travel; there was a sort of rivalry between them which resulted in better roads than would have otherwise been made. But when 'the railways came, they did away with all that. And, now, the era of automobiles is coming in, and is bringing that class of traffic back to the farmers' doors that has not been there before for a great many _ years, although it must be said that he is not very anxious sometimes to get it. But we must deal with all these questions as they arise, and they will 'have to be dealt with in this country. It is said that in the state of New York the outlay on roads will be largely repaid by the tax imposed on automobiles in that state. It seems to me that while this House has a right to deal with the matter, it will be a question to a considerable extent of co-operating with the provinces in carrying out the object of this Bill. I wish to say in conclusion that Whatever may be the outcome, I hope and believe that great good will result from this legislation to the community in general.

I think we are all agreed that the legislation which is now before the committee is per se good legislation, subject, however, to tire limitations which were formulated in "the amendment proposed by the right ihon. leader of tire opposition.
However, this amendment was lost, and we are now face to face with the legislation as introduced by the Minister of Railways and Canals. As I said a moment ago, every class in this country will readily admit that a good roads policy is a safe policy. I have always been of opinion, and this opinion is shared by many, that the provinces at the time of Confederation were not given their proper share of subsidies. They were given only limited powers and thereby limited resources. As the Mr. BRODER,
roads were more under their control than under the control of the federal authorities, the highway in the various provinces has not been what it should be. However, Sir, we must not forget that time flies, and that immediately after the old days were past, when that lonely trail was kept open by the settler, came the railway age which did away practically for at least forty years with the immediate necessity for an improved highway. People thought only of railways and of the settlement of the country through the railways. But a new era has dawned in this country, and not only in this country but on the whole of the continent. It is that of the good roads. My hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder) has referred to the state of the roads in France and England. A comparison between the roads of the old country and the roads, of the new continent cannot hold good, because the roads in France and England date as far back as the Roman conquest in some cases, and the climate on the other side contributes towards maintaining in their proper condition the highways .of both these countries. I quite agree with the hon. gentleman that there is nothing so glorious as a ride or drive on the highways of France or England, but, as I have just stated, it is impossible for Canada or even for the northern portion of the United States, to maintain roads in that condition on account of the climate. But we can imitate, even though it be at a distance, what has been done in the old country and by the richer states of the United States commonwealth. We have passed the age when railways were the exclusive necessity. We, of course, admit as a foregone conclusion that the whole country must be a network of railways, but our attention must also be turned towards the establishment and maintenance of a perfect system of highways. I do not know what has been done in the other provinces, but I can speak of what I have seen in Ontario, where a forward policy has been the aim of the government for the last twenty years. I have noticed, especially around Toronto, Hamilton and London, that they have almost reached perfection as Tegards highways. I do not know how it is in other sections or in other provinces, but the province of Ontario has had very good roads for the last twenty years. In the province of Quebec we have just inaugurated a good roads policy. The progressive administration of Sir Louis Gouin has just decided that $10,000,000 would be appropriated towards the opening and maintaining of good soads within the boundaries of the province. The municipalities are going to share in the construction and maintenance of the highways. There will be a consortium between the municipalities and the government of the province. Each will contribute its

share. No later than last week the Minister of Agriculture was given new powers by legislation for the carrying out of that policy.
I think the people only pay two per cent and then the government create a sinking fund.

Yes, that is the basis of the arrangement. I do not share the view of my hon. friend from Dundas with reference to the establishment of a federal roads system in Canada. I believe that we are almost all agreed that the money to be voted by this parliament for good roads throughout Canada should be distributed in the way suggested this afternoon by both my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) and my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). I think the Minister >f Railways should prepare a concrete plan which might be submitted to the different provinces and the moneys might then be handed to the provincial exchequers, and expended under the conditions imposed by the authority of this parliament and by the authority of the minister. 1 believe that under that system we could have shortly in Canada a splendid highway from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Mv hon. friend from Dundas stated quite rightly a moment ago that the automobile had completely changed the conditions of, shall I say, existence-in America. I know that in the old country conditions have been changed completely since the appearance of the automobile. There the leisurely class of people travel more by automobile to-day than they do by railway. People go across the Atlantic, and take their automobile with them in order to see the country that they do not see well when they travel by rail. I do not wish to be provincial, but I can apeak for my own province where I spend the summers. Even in the remote districts of Quebec, on the coast of Gaspe and at Murray Bay in the county of Charlevoix where they have no railway system, I have seen during the summer, hundreds of automobiles coming from the United States loaded with tourists, visiting our highly favoured, picturesque regions and spending money lavishly. Their visits have had a twofold result. First of all, the people have become a little more proud; they look after their gardens, their farms and keep their habitations more clean and tidy. They supply butter, cheese, fruits and other staples to the tourists and above all they are inclined to do a little more towards maintaining the roads than before. Above all the automobile has been a blessing in disguise in that we have now, in the remotest country districts, better hotel accommodation. Though the automobile is dreaded by many habitants because some horses take fright
when they see it coming, it has nevertheless been a blessing in disguise.
The advent of the automobile has unquestionably been a great inducement towards the betterment of highways, and has given us better hotel accommodation. This is Sir, a progressive policy, and provided the money we grant is not spent to debauch the electorate, but in the public interest, and with safeguards thrown around its expenditure, I believe this legislation will be most beneficial to the inhabitants of Canada.

I endorse the suggestion of the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Bro-der) that this expenditure should be on trunk line roads, and I do so all the more readily, because of our experience in British Columbia. A few years ago, Mr. Taylor, Minister of Public Works for British Columbia, conceived the idea of setting aside a certain sum of money each session for the building of a trunk road from Bur-rard Inlet to the provincial boundary of Alberta. That proposal when first made was received not only by a large number of the members of the House, but by a large number of the people of the province, with very grave doubt, fearing, as they did, that a special trunk road of that nature was scarcely warranted by the then development stage of our province. However, only two or three sessions passed before Mr. Taylor was able to demonstrate the great benefit such a trunk line bestowed on the province. Mr. Taylor is now affectionately called by the people ' Good Roads Taylor,' and there is no more popular grant made in the legislature than the annual appropriation for the continuation of that provincial trunk road. To give an idea how such a trunk road advertises the province, I may mention that last winter I delivered a lecture in Toronto and having referred to this British Columbia provincial road, a number of gentlemen waited on me after the meeting; they were men of leisure and means, and they decided to so arrange their summer tour that they might motor over that scenic route in British Columbia. I feel strongly that if this grant of Dominion money is merely distributed throughout the provinces here and there, for municipal roads, you will not get the same concrete benefit you would if the expenditure were made on a distinctive trunk line road; a road that eventually would stretch from Halifax on the Atlantic to Burrard Inlet, on the Pacific. Were such a road constructed, the municipal roads would become feeders to it, with the result that they would be greatly improved and the whole Dominion would reap untold benefits. I was present at the Yukon Exposition in Seattle, and I attended .there an illustrated lecture on good roads. One of the pictures thrown on the screen showed a team of horses with a wagon containing

two or three bales of cotton, the wagon stuck in the mud, the fences broken, and everything dilapidated and dismal looking. Then, another picture showed the same place five years after the construction of a trunk road, and on this road was a wagon loaded with a ton and a half of baled cotton, drawn by a splendid team of horses, and with fine residences on each side of the rgad. The lecturer assured us that all this change had been brought about inside of five years by the good roads improvement commission of that district, and the illustration impressed itself very vividly on my mind. It is my opinion that the municipalities should continue to look after their own roads and that the Dominion grant should be devoted to a trunk line system of roads, such as I have referred to. The trunk road would be in the nature of a model road; it would be laid out with the idea of reaching from one snecific point to another, exactly like a transcontinental line of railway, and the municipal roads would become feeders to it. I believe that is the correct principle upon which the Dominion grant should be expended. A splendid trunk road extending through the entire Dominion would be an incentive to the municipalities to put their roads in first class order; it would induce travel by tourists who would be free spenders; it would encourage the erection of first class tourist hotels at various places, and on the whole it would in every way benefit every part of the Dominion. I most heartily endorse that portion of the remarks of the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) in which he advocated this trunk line road.

I must express my absolute disapproval of the statement made by the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Good-eve) as well as by the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) in regard to a general trunk line. The hon. member for Dundas stated that many years ago municipalities in the province of Ontario borrowed money from the government under the Municipal Loan Fund Act, and that in the settlement of that indebtedness things did not work out satisfactorily. I think they worked out with absolute satisfaction. Those municipalities which had borrowed money received certain sums from the government of the province, and that money went into permanent improvements such as the building of town halls or other public buildings.
That was not done at all.

It was done in every district that I know anything about. It may not have been done in the district which the hon. gentleman comes from, because the people there may not have been as careful in the management of their affairs as they were in my section. The hon. gentleman talked of a main highway Mr. GOODBYE
through the length of this country, as though it were as important as a new trunk line of railway, paying that the money which is voted by the Dominion parliament should be applied to the construction of a main trunk line of highway from east to west, and, as the hon. member for Kootenay said, feeders built leading to that. Let me tell my hon.' friend that the good roads which the fanners of this country want are good roads leading from their farms to the railway stations in their own localities, and not good roads which lead to any trunk highway which runs from east to west, and which is built simply for the automobilist and the tourist. The farmers of this country want good roads; they are in favour of this Bill, and the Liberal party are in favour of it, because it was the Liberal party of the province of Ontario that first introduced the proposition.
Oh, oh.

Let me tell the hon. gentlemen who smile that the first good-roads legislation that was ever introduced in Canada was introduced by the government of Sir George Ross in the province of Ontario. That legislation was accepted by the succeeding government, of which the hon. Minister of Railway^ was a member. They improved on it, to some extent, I admit, because they increased the amount of the allowance to the municipalities. I want to emphasize that the money which is to be appropriated by this parliament for the construction of good roads must be devoted to the construction of good roads throughout the various municipalities in the Dominion-not to a main trunk line. When the government sees fit to appropriate money for that purpose, we will discuss that proposal when it comes. But this Bill is for the purpose of aiding the provinces in the construction of good roads under the legislative jurisdiction of the provinces and that is to aid the municipalities in building good roads for the use of the farmers generally in carrying their wheat and other products to the markets on the lines of the various railways!, and not for the construction of a main trunk line from one end of this country to the other.

I want to congratulate the government on having brought this Bill before the House. I believe the remarks made by my hon. friend who has just taken his seat are on the right line, so far as the province of Manitoba is concerned. The trunk road idea is a good one, but the roads through our different municipalities are of more importance to us at the present time. In my province we have laboured under great difficulties' for many years from the fact that we have had very

poor roads and very little money to make good ones. I have often wondered why the Dominion government did not take this matter up years ago. I know that the late government, or at least some of the ministers, were approached on different occasions, but they were afraid t-o bring the subject before the House; they said it was too great an undertaking. That was the answer that some of my friends from Manitoba got, and I want to congratulate the government to-day on having the courage to bring this measure before parliament. To my mind there is nothing that concerns the province of Manitoba more than the question of good roads. In my own county, which is nearly 150 miles square, we have been labouring under great difficulties. Indeed, throughout the whole province the question of making roads is a very difficult one, owing to tile lack of money. The provincial government has come to our aid from time to time, but owing largely perhaps to the manner in which the province has been treated for many years by the Dominion government, the funds at their disposal have been insufficient to aid us to any great extent. The consequence has been that in the settled districts after a heavy shower of rain, it is almost impossible for a loaded wagon to pass along the roads. Therefore, the proposed Bill is a blessing to the province from which I come, and I trust that there will be a well-advised scheme for giving effect to it. Some hon. members spoke of the money being handed over to the different municipalities. If I read the Bill correctly, there is no such intention. I understand that the money will be expended under a well-devised scheme between this government and the provincial governments. In that way I believe we shall obtain value for every dollar of this money. While on my feet I want to say a word about a federal road. There are some districts in Canada where I believe a distinct federal road would be justified, and I have one in my mind's eye at the present time. At Stony Mountain, about twelve miles from the city of Winnipeg, we have a large penitentiary, and ' the road between that point and Winnipeg is almost impassable. There is a daily train service, but we ought to have a federal state road between the penitentiary and the city of Winnipeg. We have a mountain of stone, and the government could construct the road cheaply by using the prison labour.
I hope the government will use that prison labour to construct between Winnipeg and Stony Mountain a first class state highway. The distance is about 12 miles. This would be in the interests of the whole community, and the employment of prison labour in the construction of roads throughout this country is highly desirable. The
section of road I have mentioned would afford a very valuable demonstration as to the practicability of this system. The material is at hand and the road could be built as a distinctive state road. I hope that a large portion of the roads for which money is provided in this Bill will be built in the different municipalities} throughout the country, especially in the province of Manitoba. For instance, a large amount of money has been spent on the road between Winnipeg and Selkirk during the last 30 or 40 years by the different municipalities, assisted by the provincial government, but it is still a very indifferent road, and I trust it will be one of the roads to receive attention. The idea of a trunk line from coast to coast is an admirable one and when the country feels it can afford the luxury of a road of that kind I will endorse the proposal as quickly as any man in the House, but at present I hope the money that is being voted will be spent to aid the farmers in getting their produce to the markets and railway stations, and the only way to do that is to spend it in the different municipalities. I want to congratulate the government on their courage in introducing this legislation, and I hope that the appropriation that is made will be a liberal one.

I am in favour of good roads, because naturally I like to drive on them. The people of Oxford county have built many first-class macadam roads under what they call the county roads system, assisted by the province. My support of this measure would depend entirely on what is proposed. One section of the Bill provides that the assistance ' shall be given upon such terms and subject to such conditions.' Does the minister mean that he will keep^ control of the money granted to the provinces to a certain extent, after it is granted? That, I think, makes a material difference. If, as has been stated by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways, the money is intended to be granted on the principle laid down by my right hon. leader- (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), then we will have no quarrel with it. As to the construction of a trunk road, if the government intend to keep some control of the construction of roads by the various provinces they could acquire a trunk road without building it themselves by seeing that the various provinces constructed roads which would connect so as to make a trunk road from province to province. I quite agree that what the farmers principally need is good roads leading to their nearest markets.
As to the benefit to the community from having a trunk road with automobiles running along it, the farmers in my sections of the country ate not so keen on having

automobiles on itheir roads; in fact, they are rather opposed to them. The ladies, who after all, should govern, are very much opposed to them, and say they cannot go out without having their horses frightened. Automobiles do a great deal of harm to macadam roads, and I wonder the provinces have not long since taxed automobiles to help construct roads. While I am not opposed to automobiles, as I like to ride in them myself on occasions, at the same time they sweep up an enormous quantity of dust, and farmers with fields adjacent to roads suffer loss from the dust raised by automobiles. I would like the Minister of Railways to consider seriously the amendment moved on the second reading by the leader of the opposition, with reference to giving the money only in the form of subsidies to 'the provinces. The movement is 'an excellent one that should receive commendation if properly carried out, but I think it dangerous to build trunk lines, and absolutely unnecessary if the government retain the .right to control tire building of roads. The money should be given to the provinces on the distinct understanding that it will be given to the municipalities, and in Ontario I think it should be given to the county councils.

What would my hon. friend do in the ease of counties that have already constructed good roads and taxed their people for them under the system spoken of by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), or with reference to the unorganized sections of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec ?
To equalize them ?
Yes.

I think the moneys could be easily expended in maintaining the roads. The provincial grants made in Ontario lack provision, which is very necessary, for the maintenance of the roads after their construction.
I know that in our section of country- and we have, I suppose, as many miles of road as any other county in the province- the provincial government assisted the county in building roads. But the great difficulty is that the roads are not maintained in any such condition a(s they should be. Now, where, it seems to me, our section could well be assisted by the Dominion, would be in seeing to it that the province made a condition that the road should be properly maintained according to a certain standard as well as being built to a standard. I may be wrong, but that would be my idea of the way to assist those who have already built roads. There is no county in Ontario, so far as I know, t-hait has built anything approaching the number of roads it required. That is one of the troubles in the sections of country Mr. NESBITT
that are building these roads-the jealousy that arises on the part of those sections which have not good roads. I do not wish to take up time, but 1 would urge my hon. friend the Minister of Railways to drop that portion of his Bill that, apparently, goes into the building of federal trunk roads.	.
We haven't come to that yet.

I know that; but, in the meantime, I hope the hon. gentleman will think it over a<nd be willing to drop that clause, so that the subsidies may go to the provinces to be spent under the control, after all, of the Dominion.

The Bill now before us is, I am sure, one of the most important that the government will bring forward this session. Especially is it important on account of the direct benefit it is going to bring to a very large proportion of the people of this country. It is a Bill which affects the interests of all classes. We often speak as though good roads affected only the farmers, but they affect far more than the farmers. Good roadis affect the people of -every village, town and city. They affect the welfare of the workingman and business iman -as well as that of the farmer. Good roads will tend to lessen the cost of living in our urban centresi. Some years ago, when many of our towns had a population of 4,000 or 5,000, the people could be 'supplied with farm produce by the farmers living within a radius of five or six miles. But many of these towns, especially in the province of Ontario, have grown so that they have a population of ten to fifteen thousand. The result is that the farmer living within a reasonable radius are unable to -supply all the produce which is required. Unless a farmer lives within seven or eight miles of the centre, he finds it too expensive to market his -produce in that center biy driving -over a road which is not in good condition. The result is that the middleman is coming in. Produce is being brought to the former by train, and the workingman in these centres is being compelled to buy the farmer's produce not from the farmer direct, but from the middleman with the middleman's profit added. The greater portion of the municipal taxation of the present day is levied for the purpose of building and maintaining roads. So much is this the case, that we find the farmers of Ontario 'labouring under a heavy burden of -taxes. We may not say so much about the burden of the farmers of Ontario as some of our western friends say about the burdens of the western farmers, but none the less it is a fact that municipal taxation in Ontario to-day is becoming

very heavy. Anything which will assist in lessening that taxation, anything that will alleviate to some extent the burdens of the farmers in that regard will be received with a great deal of favour by them. I have just said that the greater part of the taxation inf municipalities to-day is raised for the purpose of building roads. Yet, notwithstanding that, w-e find that the municipalities are often unable to raise sufficient ito construct permanent roads. The result is that the roads throughout our province generally, are not improving at anything like the rate they should improve with the vast amount of money that is spent annually upon them. The cost of labour is increasing and we find to-day, notwithstanding the generous aid given by the Ontario government to the municipalities of that province, that the taxation levied upon the farmer is just as great or greater than it was when She road system of 'Ontario was inaugurated. So while the assistance given has in a measure relieved the burden, it has not reduced the cost which is levied upon the farmer. This is, therefore, an opportune time for the Dominion government to come to the aid of the agricultural population in this way and assist them in maintaining the roads that they require.
I am not in sympathy at all.with those who talk of building trunk lines. Every municipality to-day is labouring and wrestling with the problem of how to build and maintain their roads without raising the taxation on their farms to too great a degree. That is a need which is urgent not only in one section of the country, but, I bellieve, in all sections. And it seems to me that it becomes the duty of the government first to relieve the urgent needs of the farmer. Therefore, the first duty of the government in granting aid to roads, I think, is to give aid in such a way as will relieve the municipality of at least a portion of the cost of constructing and maintaining roads. Trunk roads may be all right after a few years., but the time has not yet come when the people are demanding that. What benefit would a trunk road be to the great mass of the farmers of any of our provinces? It might assist those living along that road; but I doubt very much, espe-cilly if a trunk road is to be used solely by the automobiles, that the farmers living along that road will receive it with favour, for we find that those living adjacent t-o roads most travelled by automobiles say that their crops are being injured -by the dust caused by the traffic. In addition to those living along the road, a trunk iroad might aid those living within ten or twelve miles of it. But we know that farmers living beyond that radius will
benefit little or none. Farmers are not travelling fifteen, twenty or thirty miles to market as they did years ago. Every farmer has a market, town within ten or twelve miles of his farm; and the road he wants improved is the road he is using from his farm to the market town.
I am sure that while we appreciate the value of the tourist travel in Canada, and while there are many counties in every province that are attractive to th-e tourist, I hardly think the country is at present prepared to enter upon the task of building roads for the purpose of encouraging tourists to visit Canada. I think that our most pressing need at present is to build roads for the benefit of the farmers. I hope that whatever aid is granted will be expended in such a manner as to benefit the townships and counties, to aid the farmer who is anxious to have good roads, and who is willing to pay generously to build and maintain them. At the same time, we know that he needs assistance, not only from the provincial governments but from the Dominion government, and for that reason I am in favour of this Bill.

The question which seems to engage the attention of members on both sides of the House is how best to apply this money so as to get the most benefit out of it for the Canadian people. I had the pleasure the other day of attending the Good Roads Convention in this city; a majority of the representatives were from the province of Ontario. A great many of the delegates expressed their views with regard to good roads, and it was the unanimous opinion of the convention that this money should not be expended in building trunk lines throughout the province, or throughout the Dominion. When that deputation appeared in this Chamber before the Prime Minister and some other members of the Cabinet, they were addressed by five or six persons, the majority of whom represented the cities, the manufacturers and the motormen of Canada. The president of the Motormen's Association, in the course of his remarks, said that our roads were generally in a deplorable condition, -that they were greatly in need of improvement, and he also favoured the system of building trunk lines throughout the country The argument of the representative of the Manufacturers' Association was along the same line. The only sound views, in my estimation, were given in the address of the president of the Good Roads Association. He expressed his confidence that the government would expend this money in road building so as to make it of general benefit to the coun.try districts.
Some hon. members to-night have

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few general observations regarding the Bill which is now before the committee. I suppose it is unnecessary for me to say anything as to the value of good roads, , for I imagine that we
will all be in unison upon this question. There is no doubt that highways have been the greatest element in the civilization of countries. Nothing can promote commerce to a greater degree than good highways, and, perhaps better still, nothing tends to give to a country greater social and national contentment than a good system of highways. The intrusion, however, of the federal parliament into a public service which has heretofore been cared for altogether by the provinces is, as has been stated, a new departure and it raises problems, many of which, I think, will be found by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) and the government, difficult to solve. However, I am sure that hon. gentlemen in this House will agree that if any workable method can be devised of assisting the provinces in securing good or better highways than they have now, the measure before the House will meet with commendation from everybody in it and from the country generally. Great care should be exercised in working out any system, and I think that on the occasion of the introduction of this Bill by the Minister of Railways he spoke as one who felt that it was a very difficult task to prepare a suitable Bill. ' If I may make a suggestion-not thas I expect it to be carried out-I would say that the government might very well have taken the months which will intervene between the closing of this session and the opening of next session and devoted the time to the study of this question and to conferences with the several provinces, so that at the next session they would have been able to have presented to parliament a Bill containing a definite scheme. Had this been done it would have been more satisfactory to parliament and to the country generally. Of course, it was to be expected of the government that they would, at the earliest possible moment, implement the pledge which they made to the country during the recent campaign, namely, to grant financial aid to the provinces towards highway improvement. But I am sure that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House and the country generally would have favourably considered a statement from the government to the effect that before introducing this legislation they desired time to consider the whole subject.	It would have been very
much in the interest of parliament and the country and possibly to the betterment of our highways, had the government devoted a little moTe time to the study of the question with its many problems and presented their decision at the next session of parliament. I think I can venture the statement that it is highly improbable that any work can be done upon the highways of any province during

the year 1912. After the closing of parliament, conferences must take place with the several provinces, and when these conferences commence many problems will arise which none of us perhaps foresee to-night. The discussion this evening upon this Bill discloses the fact that hon. gentlemen entertain many different views.
I therefore, believe it will be impossible for the provinces and the federal government to reach a working agreement and to form an organization which will carry out any scheme of expenditure ultimately agreed upon between the Dominion Government and the several provinces. I venture the opinion that there can be no expenditure of moneys by the federal government for the year' 1912, which will go to the provincial governments. If there is, I do feel it will not be profitably expended for the reason that no well-thought out scheme will be possible of attainment in such a short time. While the expenditure of federal moneys upon the public highways is a new thing in this country, I do not think for my part that it will be objectionable. The financial strength of the several provinces is limited indeed and I think before many years the federal government will find that they must, for different reasons, augment the provincial subsidies. In the United States this matter has been frequently discussed. In the early days of the history of the United States, that country did embark in the building of trunk lines, notably one known as the Cumberland Road, starting from the headwaters of the Potomac River in Maryland, going through Pennsylvania and West Virginia to Ohio, and that road was completed in 1805. The federal government constructed ten or twelve other roads, but no great expenditure was made and after the Civil War that policy ended. These roads were constructed largely for military purposes, and while many requests have been made of recent years upon the United States federal government for expenditure on highways, so far nothing has been done. They have however a Good Roads Bureau in Washington which is doing excellent service. I would like to read from an article by a magazine writer, upon improved highways, the following short extract concerning the good roads work done by the United States Government.
Foremost of these outside agencies is the United States office of public roads organized in 1893 with an appropriation of $14,000, with offices in two attic rooms. This bureau has increased in usefulness until now it occupies a four story building of its own which includes within its walls, physical, chemical, petrographic and photographic laboratories and a machine shop, and has at its disposal an appropriation of $116,000. A staff of twenty-four engineers and superintendents of road construction are employed to teach the art Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
of road building to any community that will take the trouble to ask for their services and provide ithe material and labour. A favourite feature of the bureau is the object lesson road project. This consists in assigning an engineer to supervise the construction of a short section of road to demonstrate the proper methods aand instruct local builders. Up to July 1st, 1909, 264 object lesson roads had been built in thirty-five states, demonstrating the proper methods of using crushed stone, sand, clay, shell, earth, bituminous materials and brick. Besides this, the engineers of the bureau give special advice, deliver technical lectures, introduce model systems of construction, maintenance and administration in counties and study and report on practical methods for a series of years.
That is as far as the United States have gone in the way of assisting public highways, although demands have been made for direct contribution to the several states as is contemplated by this measure. However, I believe that public opinion is travelling very rapidly in the United States at present upon the question of improved highways, and that the federal government will ultimately come to the aid of the states possibly in the manner contemplated by the Bill now before the committee. In other countries* of the world in which the federal system does not prevail direct expenditures of moneys are made for the improvement of highways by the government. As has been staged, by the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) we find an illustration of this in France, which spends seven million dollars annually upon its highways. There are four systems of roads in France; the national roads which are built and maintained by the state; the military roads, which are maintained by the state; the departmental roads which would correspond to the county roads in this country, and which are maintained by the state and by the department themselves, and the communal roads, which correspond to the ordinary highways in this country, and which are maintained by the people. In England and Wales fifteen million dollars are spent annually upon highways, and, according to the magazine writer from whom I quoted a moment ago, one hundred and sixty million dollars annually are expended _ by fourteen nations of Europe upon their highways. Now, while the House will cordially support this measure and will give to the government every assistance to extend to the country the benefits of this measure, still in this departure of financial aid to the provinces for highway improvements we should exercise caution. Personally, I regret very much that the government have seen fit to deal with the Bill this year. I would never, for my part, have censured them for not presenting to parliament such a measure at this session. In

fact I will go as far as to say that they have, hardly given us a measure at all because the Bill before the House is hardly worthy of the name of a Bill. I approve of the preamble and that is probably the best part of it. But I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite must agree with me that the Bill is very indefinite, that it discloses no plan and no matured, scheme and that everything indicates that the government have so far, given little, if any attention to the principle involved in the Bill. I do not criticise the government for that. I recognize the fact that since their advent to power, they collectively and individually have been very busy, but I think they should realize that in embarking upon a policy of Federal expenditure in connection with roads in this country, they are adopting a policy which is new to Canada, which involves many important questions, and I think they might have well asked parliament and the country to give them a few months to enable them further to study the measure before presenting it to this House.
Now, let me point out some of the matters which should be considered in connection with this Bill. Section 3 says that the Governor in Council may grant money in any year to any province. That is hardly satisfactory legislation. 'It breaks every canon of legislation with Tegard to the expenditure of moneys. It is not the practice to give legislative powers to the Governor in Council in matters of this kind. Then I think we should know approximately what sum of money the government propose devoting to roads in the various provinces. It inust be a very substantial sum or it will 'be of no use. It is important also to know how many years this expenditure will continue-whether it will be perpetuity or for 'a fixed number of years. I understand that the government of Nova Scotia propose to expend money on capital account 'for road improvement in the very near future; and if they knew definitely what 'sum of money they would get from this government, and over what period it would continue. I am sure that it would affect their policy materially. There are many other questions which it is important to consider in connection with the expenditure of money for the improvement of our highways. We should have some information as to the total mileage of the roads in the several provinces. There should be some classification of these roads. There should be some standardization of the work that is to be performed. There will be the question of maintenance, which is far more important than construction and involves more difficulties. I venture to think that it will require many months to develop a method
of expenditure which will be acceptable to the government itself, to. parliament, and to the country; it will take a long time to reach an agreement with the several provinces; and I am sure that if the government appealed even to their own supporters in parliament, they would find many varieties of opinion as to the form this expenditure should take. I trust, however, that if the government decide to proceed with the expenditure this season, which I very much doubt, they will be able to develop a policy and a system of expenditure which will meet with the concurrence of hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House. I trust that they will not pay very much attention to the suggestion of a trunk line from coast to coast. We may possibly reach such a thing some day, but in view of the present condition of the ordinary highways of the country, I think I can say with consider-' able confidence that the suggestion of a federal road from coast to coast would not meet with very much favour. There is this to be remembered, however, that as our highways in the several provinces are improved by a better system of construction, reconstruction and maintenance, gradually the scheme of a national highway from coast to coast will develop itself. Neither do I favour the idea of giving this money to any municipality, for the reason that I think experience teaches that the expenditure would not be made by any municipality in such a way as to secure permanent results. If the money proposed to be granted under this measure were given to the municipalities, I believe that it would not be expended in accordance with any system. The provincial governments would be better equipped to make the expenditure, and they can better than any municipality rise above local considerations.
Mr. HENDERSON, I have not given this matter very great consideration, but of all the municipal expenditures throughout the country nothing pleased me more than an expenditure for providing good roads. I am sure that the people are coming more and more every year to appreciate good roads.
The objection to municipal taxation for the improvement of roads which we heard in bygone days is gradually being removed. The advantages of good roads in country places is so much appreciated by the ordinary public that I do not think any objection can be found in Canada against the measure proposed by the government.
I appreciate the efforts the government are making on behalf of the people to provide a good roads system. I want to endorse

their action, to give it my sanction, and to say that in the part of the country which I represent I believe their action will be heartily endorsed. Nothing so strikes our attention in the old land as the admirable roads, founded I suppose on a basis that was laid by the Romans in the olden times. These roads are repaired yearly, Dractically they are never allowed to get out of repair, and so the cost of repair is light, while the people always have good roads It may be said that this measure is immature, but the government are making a beginning, people will begin to talk about good roads as they are proposed to be developed by the Dominion government, or through the provincial governments, or municipalities, whatever system may be adopted, and in that way the government will gradually get a great deal of information that will assist them in maturing their scheme. I, therefore, think they were wise in bringing down this measure at tins early date. Very much cannot be done this year, but a start has been made, and I look forward in the near future to a great improvement in the scheme which is as yet only in its infancy. I have never known any measure to receive such cordial support in this House. There may be differences of opinion as to the time and methods of carrying out this proposal, but on the principle of improving the highways of the country I believe both sides of the House are unanimous in heartily supporting the Bill.

This question -affects almost every one in Canada. It must be satisfactory to the government to realize the approval that has been manifested throughout the country, and by those who have spoken on this question to-night. Since the most primitive times the highway has been of the most vital importance to every one. The foot-passenger in years gone by considered that when he was on the King's highway he was safe, and as time went on he was by statue compelled to .go oust and help to construct a highway that would meet the requirements of the country. We have reached the time when it is necessary not only for the provincial governments to do something towards building and maintaining the highways, but for the federal government to relieve the burdens of the people in this respect. It has been said to-night that the civilization of a people can be judged from the standard of their highways. This is quite possible. The hon. member for Rouville said that we have passed the railway age, and must now devote our attention to building better highways. It struck me at the time what a welcome such a system as this would have received from the people of 80 to 100 years ago, the system that has been Mr. HENDERSON.
advocated by several speakers, that is a provincial or federal highway, east and west from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Happily we are living in an -age of progress, and I believe the day has passed when any such system as that is required in this country. The roads radiating from the different .market centres throughout Canada are the roads that ought to receive the greatest attention. I believe the statements made here to-night to that effect are an echo of articles that have been appearing in the public pmess for some, time past and that we may nest assured that those articles have bean inspired by those who desire the bonstruction of a great oon-timnous highway from the Atlantic to the Pacific for a specific purpose. I do not believe that such a system would meet the requirements of the people to the same extent as roads radiating out from these different points. If that were the intention of the government in this Bill I would be opposed to it. If such a system of roads as that were to be constructed the government ought to buy a right of w.a|y and build a road of that kind because it certainly would be monopolized for three or four months of the year by the automobilists to the exclusion of those using horse vehicles. If such a system of highways were built it should be built apart from our present highways, it should be built on a right-of-way acquired for the purpose; where you could turn the automobiles loose and let them run as fast as they like, where they would not interfere with other people. I believe that such a Toad for the use of automobiles would have to be of different construction from any road yet built in the rural districts of Canada. The very best macadiam-roadis in our country have been absolutely ruined in three or four years by automobile traffic. On a dusty summer day an automobile travelling at the rate of forty or fifty miles an hour raises a cloud of dust that settles anywhere between twenty and forty rods of that road. The unfortunate people who live within a few rods of a highway are made very uncomfortable through having to keep their windows closed to keep out the dust. For that reason I contend that if such a system is intended it should be a road constructed of material that would not be drawn up by the suction of the tires of an automobile and sent broadcast over the country.
Now, I desire to say a word about the tourists. We certainly welcome the tourists to our country; we are glad to see them come here. And, as a rule they are people who have time on their hands and are not necessarily as much hurried as those who have business pressing upon them. You notice how the automobile is becoming very fashionable during the past few years. But the rage at present seems

to be not to travel over our rural roads, but to travel through the air. We do not know how long it will be before these tourists will not require our roads at all, and I do not know but that we ought to take that into consideration. Another feature of this road situation is this, that for four or five months in the year it does not matter what the nature of that road is. We have a coating over our roads now, and have had for months, which makes it not very material whether those roads are constructed of macadam, asphalt, clay or gravel. For about two or three months in each year it is important that we should have good roads, but for the balance of the season it is not of such great importance.
I believe the government, are to be commended for endeavouring to relieve the pressure resting upon the people of this country for the building and maintaining of roads. I believe that a great deal of money has been wasted, and worse than wasted, through the manner in which it has been expended on our highways. If, through the influence of the government a more scientific mode of road construction can be adopted, a great deal will have been accomplished., But it is in the maintenance of the roads that the greatest work can be done. I believe our municipal councils, many of them, would do a great deal better if they would expend double the money they do in maintaining and looking after the roads. I believe also that the narrow-tyred wagons hauling heavy loads over our roads do more to spoil those roads than anything else. If the government would encourage the use of wide tyres on wagons-I suppose that is outside the scope of the federal government, but perhaps something could be done-a great step towards the better maintenance of our roads would be taken. These narrow tyres cut up the roads, let the water into them, and so the frost gets in two or three feet deep where there is an upheaval, and consequently the roads are thrown out of balance.
It is argued here that the government is too hasty, that there are bound to be delays before anything can be done. But is it not therefore, all the more important to pass, this Bill, so that the initial stages of this movement may be accomplished? Then, when the Dominion and provincial government authorities get together they will find out what difficulties there are and how they are to be overcome. But I do not think any difficulty will arise that cannot be overcome. All the details will have to be worked out; and then it will come before the House and it will be time enough to deal with the question. I am heartily in favour of the grants to 'be made.
I do not know that it is necessary for us to know at this stage, just how much is to 117	[DOT]
be spent or how many miles of road is to be constructed. That will all come out in good time. The improvement of rural highways is something that needs encouragement. At the same time, I must express my strongest disapproval of the views that have been expressed by a number of members to-night with regard to trunk roads. I think the day has long passed, with our present network of railways, when anything of that kind is required.
