0. GUILBAULT (Joliette) (Translation). Mt. Chairman, I have had great pleasure in listening to the speech of the horn, member for Montcalm, whose constituency adjoins mine. However one thing surprises me: his pluck which I thought was great and indomitable, has failed him entirely. He is afraid of automobiles; he considers them a calamity. I should have judged that he *would welcome with joy the building of fine highways' in the counties of Joliette and Montcalm. My wish is that the county of Joliette be provided with good roads, and even that visitors may be seen touring over them in their automobiles.
It rather confuses me to hear the hon. gentleman .state that the bill under consideration is an infringement on provincial rights, seeing that while it provides granting assistance to the provinces, it is not. until an agreement has been entered info with the provincial governments. I cannot see any encroachment when such a course is adopted.
The bon. member asks for a list of all roads which are to receive help from the government. However, has- he considered that a great deal of work would be implied in such a task? To point out all the roads which require improvements throughout the country would be an impossibility; as that would actually mean almost a book, for the counties of Montcalm and Joliette alone.
No, what the government intends to do,
I understand, is to improve existing roads, so that farmers may find it 'easier to move about in the wet season of spring and autumn. What the government intends to do is to put county towns in closer touch with the adjoining country, to help on agriculture by (facilitating assistance at fairs and agricultural competitions, through the building of good roads.
If it were proposed to build a great commercial highway between Montreal and Quebec, I do not think it would be necessary, as suggested by the member for Montcalm, to have a referendum to find out whether the farming community would approve of such a plan. Well, that is exactly what the government intends to give us, with the approval and [DOT]aid of the provincial governments. Automobiles may be (safely met on such a road, and besides, I believe farmers' sons are not quite so anxious as the member for Montcalm suggested to be provided with automobiles.
I was pleased to listen to his address, and I think others were pleased also. I

shall be happy to give my support to the government's proposal. For a long time past we were met with the cry: What are you about, are you mot going to do something towards the improvement of the roads? Now this government had pledged itself, at tire very opening of the session, to introduce a measure to that effect, and I am happy to see that it has redeemed its pledge. When I visit my constituency, and possibly that of my ban. friend for Montcalm, I shall be happy to be able to state that all Iron, members, whatever their party ties, have acknowledged the desirability of helping on the farming community and of developing the resources of tire "ount-ry through the building of good roads.

There are some points on which I think the minister ought to give us further information. I would like to know whether he is to define the classes of roads on which the money is to be expended. We are aware that in this country there are a great many roads on which provincial and municipal authorities are spending money. So far as I understood the minister's statement, he has not given ns much information on that question, I think it is very material to know whether this money is to be spent haphazard on all kinds of roads, or whether the government intends to define the classes of roads on which it will be expended. Then with regard to the maintenance of highways after they are built, another question on which the minister lias given us insufficient information. Is it the intention of the government not only to construct these highways but also to maintain them; or is it the intention to oast the burden of their maintenance on the municipalities? That is also a pertinent question. Again, the matter of bridges has not been referred to in the discussion; I do not know that it has been mentioned at all. In my province of Nova Scotia the question of permanent structures 'across streams is a very important one. - The province of Nova Scotia has borrowed the .sum of $2,000,000, and has expended that money in the construction of steel and iron bridges throughout the province. Now, is it the intention of the government to spend 'any part of this money in the construction of bridges across streams ? These questions are all of interest, on which I would like to have the views of the minister before I am asked to vote. I may say that I aim heartily in favour of expenditures of this kind on roads throughout the country. There is nothing so much needed in the county I have the honour to represent as good roads. The Bill, so far as it will tend to the improvements of roads, will have my hearty approval.
The clause that has been discussed a Mr. GU1LBATJLT.
good deal this evening, namely, clause 6, is the one to which I take especial .objection. I was disappointed that the minister did not adopt the suggestion of the right bon. leader of the opposition and frankly say that this money would be distributed according to the population of each province. There is -anotner method that might be adopted, and that is the mileage of the roads and which I think perhaps would be the fairer method. At all events, we are accustomed to the principle that moneys given to the provinces should be given according to population, and I would suppose that on so elementary a matter the minister would have no hesitation in adopting that principle. I do not see why he refuses to adopt it. If money is to be awarded to the various provinces it should certainly be awarded on some principle, and that principle ought to be contained in the Bill.
Does the hon. gentleman consider that mileage is a true -basis? If so, why does he consider the other principle elementary?

I would be willing to adopt either basi-s. But for my part, I would favour the mileage system. In certain localities the other principle would not work out fairly. At present I am not prepared to say which principle would work out best throughout the Dominion. My province is cut up with rivers and streams, which makes it necessary to build roads in many places on both sides of the river. In some counties there is great mileage of road compared with the size of the county; this great mileage is necessary, and perhaps such a county would not receive its fair share if the sum was divided according to population. But why should the minister refuse to place that in the Bill ? We -are told by the Prime Minister that the appropriation will define the -amount that is to be given to each province. Now that is a very haphazard way of settling it. The appropriation is made every year. The government may divide the money on that -principle this year, and may retain the principle of population; but some future government may not do that. It strikes me that one of the first things that ought to be laid down specifically in this Bill is the principle on which the money should be given to the various provinces. The provinces -all contribute alike, I suppose to the revenues of this country according to population.

Surely the hon. gentleman does not -suggest that alll the present provinces contribute -alike -on the basis of population ?
Mr. 'SINCLAIR. I think so.
They do not.
I think it will be admitted by everybody' that the provinces contribute to the revenue of the country according to population.
The provinces ruainiy contribute according to the amount they consume, because the revenue is mainly made up from the customs duties.

Quite true, and taking the country all over, I suppose the consumers in one province consume as in a like proportion. A thousand consumers in the various provinces consume much as a thousand in another province. I do not think my hon. friend will deny that the provinces contribute according to population to the revenues of this country, and that if money is to be taken from the public treasury, and awarded to the provinces for the purpose of building roads, it ought to be awarded on that principle. Now, if it is a good principle it ought to be embodied in the Bill; otherwise the division will be made, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster), would say, according to the rule of thumb. Then in order to be of service to the country, in order that we may know how much we can depend upon each year, there ought to be a stated sum. For example, at the present time the municipalities have to take the responsibility, or the provinces if you like, of maintaining and building roads. They would like to know how much they are to receive from me federal treasury in order that they might make their plans, and decide what improvements they can afford to undertake. Of course, if you are to build roads throughout Canada and make them permanent, it is a very large undertaking. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), stated that there were 50,000 miles of roads in the province of Ontario. He calculated that $2,000 a mile would build roads in that province. I do not agree with him at all, I think that figure is too low. In my own province I believe it would take at least $3,000 a mile to build and maintain a macadamized road, or to build a road1 lhat would be an approach to a macadamized road; it would take $3,000 at least. If that is true for the province of Ontario, you would require $150,000,000 to build roads over the province of Ontario, and make them permanent. You would require $60,000,000 in the little province from which I come; and taking the country all over it means that an immense sum of money would be required. It strikes me, therefore, that the government will not be able to grapple with this great question for a number of years to come. That makes it all the more necessary that they should define just what they are undertaking to do, that they
should lay down some principle on which they propose to act, in order that each province may get its fair share of the benefit of the expenditure. As I said before, the question of bridges ought to be dealt with too. They are very much required in some of the provinces. The provincial governments aie at present constructing these bridges. What does the present Bill mean so far as bridges aref concerned? I trust that when the minister addresses the House again he' will deal with that question, and inform us whether the government is going to undertake the construction of bridges.
But my main purpose m rising was to object to the provisions of clause 6. I regard that clause as very objectionable. In the first place, it involves a divided authority, it involves an expenditure of money by order in council under the control of this government. It also involves an expenditure under the control of the local government. Now, a divided authority is not good in the construction of roads. One party will be throwing it off on the other, whereas, the responsibility should be under one authority.
But divided authority was all right when the hon. gentleman's party in power was appointing fishery inspectors throughout the province. .

I am not now dealing with fishery inspection. We have no divided authority in my province. But I wanted to say something to the Prime Minister, if he were present. In the province of Nova Scotia the leader of the Conservative party in local politics, for the last twenty years has been preaching to us that we ought to have the administration road money under one authority. _ _
In that province we had the municipalities constructing the roads, we also had the local government constructing the roads and there was a conflict of authority which has not worked out well in Nova Scotia. Very recently the duty was taken from the municipalities and given to the local government with the exception of the expenditure under the statute labour law of the province. If we are to have money expended by the counties, by the provinces and by this government we will have three authorities in Nova Scotia looking after 'our roads. That is an undesirable system and if we retain clause 6 in this Bill we will have that system. I object to clause 6 because I submit that it will be a constant temptation to the government to use this money for an election fund. I see that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) laughs at that, but let me tell, him that we have had the spectacle within the last few days of a minister of

the Crown wading through the snow banks of South Renfrew peddling out road commissions in order to get votes. Does the hon. gentleman think it is fair to presume upon the moral rottenness of the people of this country?

I may say to the hon. member for Peterborough that I was much pleased to know that these corrupt proposals did not work in South Renfrew, that the people rejected them and that the leading Conservative paper in that municipality denounced and reproved the Minister of Customs for what he had done. nection with the administration of the various services of the government necessitates provision being made,for the obtaining of additional revenues to meet the requirements, and a measure dealing with this question will be presented to the House.

One disadvantage which the province of Nova Scotia has suffered for a considerable length of time, and, I presume, it is one that is in a measure common to all the provinces of Canada, is in reference to the state of the roads. We believe we have there splendid opportunities for those who desire to secure homes in Nova Scotia, but one of the disadvantages we are confronted with, is the condition of the roads, and this legislation which proposes to assist very materially in improving that condition, unfortunately does not meet with a very hearty reception from hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. What is the objection which they are urging in this connection? It is simply that the government at this time does not give details as to how this money shall be expended. I do not think that is a very serious charge. I do not think that the government should at this time, say how this money is to be expended, nor do I think it is necessary that particulars in connection with the expenditure of the money, which the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), has requested, should be given at this time. The hon. member for Guysborough has said that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane), who has charge of this legislation, should state to

this committee how this money is to be given to each of the various provinces of Canada. That was stated by both my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) and the Minister of Railways and Canals, when this legislation was introduced into this House. It was understood, and it is understood, by every fair minded man in this House, I think, that this money is to be distributed amongst the various provinces, practically upon the same basis as the subsidies to the provinces are paid. I do not think that any person who is prepared to consider the matter fairly can say that this is not a reasonable and proper manner in which to distribute the money. The bon. member for Guysborough finds fault because the Bill does not say that certain sums of money are to be expended upon the bridges of the various provinces. The Bill leaves that very largely in the hands of the governments of the different provinces to deal with.
A road would include a bridge, would it not?

I think that it would, but anyway, I take the ground that under this Bill the legislature of any province of Canada that desires to do^business on business principles with the government of the Dominion, will have no difficulty whatever in securing its fair and reasonable share of the money that is proposed to be devoted to roads and these legislatures can do with that money, in connection with the construction of roads and highways that, which, in their judgment, under the agreement is fit and just.	_
But we find that there is a very distinct difference in the opinions of hon. gentlemen opposite, upon the other side of the House, with regard to the cost of the construction of highways, and from the province of Nova Scotia we have had two opinions this afternoon with regard to that matter. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) considered that $2,000 per mile would be sufficient to construct permanent roads in the province, while my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) thinks that $3,000 per mile will be necessary. And although there is this diversity of opinion between these two gentlemen in respect to this one particular subject, yet they expect the government to come down now and say how every dollar of this money will be expended in all the various provinces throughout the Dominion. Nothing could be more unreasonable and nothing could more pointedly show the partisan spirit in which they are considering this proposed legislation. I have noticed that throughout this whole discussion every hon. gentleman on the other side of the House, no matter in what state of mind he approached the consideration
of this measure, always came to the final conclusion that he was not prepared to oppose it in any way, shape or form. Every one of these gentlemen came, so to speak, with the intention of cursing the legislation, but before they concluded their remarks we found them blessing it. There is not one of them who dares to vote against this measure, because they know that the fair-minded people of Canada are going to support it and to support the administration which has implemented one of its preelection measures this early in its career.
I believe that the farmers and those who are general users of the highways will declare that in the initiation of this legislation the government of this country has taken an advanced step. I believe that in submitting this Bill to parliament the government will meet with the unanimous en-dorsation of all reasonable and fair-minded people in Canada.

I did not intend to join in this discussion, but the debate has taken such a trend that in justice to the people I represent I must make a few observations upon the measure. I regret that the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) found it necessary to drag political issues into the discussion of such a measure. He wanted the world to understand that Nova Sootia is in a deplorable state financially. Well, there is no evidence, public or private, upon which the hon. gentleman can base that statement with any degree of certainty. The only thing he could quote in support of his statement was a press despatch, which has no authenticity whatever. All I have to say to the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) and to this House and to the country generally is that the revenues and financial standing of the province of Nova Scotia are on a better foundation to-day than ever before. The observations of the hon. member (Mr. Jameson) compel me to review to some extent the relations of the party to which he belongs in that province towards the financial condition of Nova Scotia. Nova Scotia has the unique record of having been governed by Liberals for the last forty-five years, except for one four years of the Thompson-Holmes government, which stands forth as a bare spot in the desert, as a pelican in the wilderness. At the end of the four yeaTS of the Conservative government in Nova Scotia the revenues of that province amounted only to $500,000, while to-day, through the various legitimate means which were taken by the Liberal administration, the revenue is fast approaching the two million dollar mark. And, what is the record of the Tory party in Nova Scotia in regard to every measure taken by the Liberal government to put that province on a sound financial basis? When Mr. Fielding took steps to bring

about the consolidation of the mines and to raise the royalty on coal at different stages from seven and a half cents to twelve and a half cents a ton, the Conservatives fought that proposal at every stage; they said that the coal business of Nova Scotia would be runied if the royalty were raised in that way.

Cut it out.
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER, I fear that the hon. gentleman is not speaking to the question before the Chair.

Some hon. gentleman fold me to cut it out, but I do not know what he means exactly by that, because I cannot cut out what I have said already, and I do not know by what process I could cut out what I have not yet given expression to. I will be very brief, Mr. Chairman, if you will pardon me. You were kind enough to allow me to go thus far, and I want to point out, that the revenue from coal in Nova Scotia was brought to its present excellent condition in the teeth of opposition from the Tory party. We got $675,000 from the eastern extension award, and thait. we fought for in the teeth of the Tory party, both in Ottawa and Nova Scotia. We got better terms for the province of Nova Scotia, as well as other provinces of the Dominion, through negotiations conducted by the Liberal government in Nova Scotia with the Liberal government in Ottawa, All of these things were fought by the Tory party, to which my hon. friend from Digby belongs. Therefore, if Nova Scotia has a good financial standing to-day, we have nothing to thank the Tory party for. That is all I have to say about the remarks malde by the hon. member for Digby.

Does the hon. gentleman deny that in the speech from the Throne at the opening of the Nova Scotia legislature, an intimation was given that some means would have to be taken to raise additional revenue to meet the increased expenditures of the province?
The province of Nova Scotia is going along at very rapid strides.
Will the hon. gentleman answer the question?

And in providing for these new departures in which the province of Nova Scotia is launching forth, keeping the lead educationally and otherwise of every province in the Dominion, I suppose the Premier of Nova Scotia finds it necessary to take steps to add to the revenues of that province. But that is not because there is anything the matter with the financial standing of the province, if they choose to keep within the narrow compass
which no doubt the hon. member for Digby would prescribe for them.
Does the hon. gentleman not admit that what I said is absolutely correct?

I do not admit anything of the kind. I do not know what is in the address at the opening of the Nova Scotia legislature, I did not see it, and I am not going to commit myself or my friends to press despatches which do not give the text of the address at all.
The Premier of Nova Scotia last summer told me in conversation that there were some sources in the province which should contribute something towards the revenue, and it is possible he is going to take steps to bring about such a condition as he had in mind, not because of lack of prosperity in the province, but in order to secure contributions to the revenue from sources which are not contributing at present. When my hon. friend comes to deal with the matter, I think he will find that this is not from any urgency for a fair distribution throughout the province of the collection of the moneys necessary for the different purposes which come within the purview of the provincial government.

Do I understand that the hon. gentleman favours deferring to 'another year the payment to the province of Nova Scotia of any portion of the money proposed by this legislation to be distributed amongst the various provinces?

I am certainly in favour of a fair contribution to the provinces along the lines suggested in this Bill, but I am disposed to agree with the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) that the government should be in possession of some further information before dealing with this Bill. When the Bill is passed, as it no doubt will pass, and when the hon. Minister of Railways or some representative of his department goes with that Bill in his hands to negotiate with one of the provincial governments, I think he will have very insufficient 'and meagre material with which to negotiate. If the negotiations had taken place first and the conditions and circumstances had been known to the minister, I think a better Bill could have been framed. I do not think the passing of the Bill at this session of parliament will hasten things very much, if clause 6 is permitted to remain in the Bill, because it evidently contemplates some legislation by the legislatures of the different provinces before anything can be done. I think it is a fair assumption that before this Bill becomes law, the legislatures of the different provinces will have prorogued, and there

will be no opportunity of implementing this Bill by provincial legislation this year. If this is the -case, there would not be very much lost if the government adopted the course suggested by the hon. member for Halifax. Some of us have the misfortune to be lawyers, and when, we come to deal with questions involving constitutional considerations, we wish to keep as much as possible within constitutional lines. Some hon. gentlemen may think that it is not very difficult to take any amount of money and spend it on the roads of the different provinces. If the hon. Minister of Railways had come today with a Bill asking that a certain amount of money should be devoted to education in the different provinces, it 'would strike us at once that he was up against a difficult situation, because it is well understood that education is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces; but when you come to look at the provisions of the constitution under which we live, you find that roads and education are in precisely the same condition, both being under the exclusive control of the provincial legislatures.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If that is correct, how was it that the previous government was justified in appointing a commission for. the purpose of investigating and reporting on the whole question of technical education?

That is quite easy, and if this government had taken the precaution to appoint one of their numerous and prolific commissions to inquire into the condition of the roads, they would have been able to offer a better Bill. The outgoing government wanted to know whether it would be advisable or not to depart from the beaten path with regard to education, and to appropriate some money for the advancement of technical education in this country, and for the building of institutions devoted to technical education. I am proud to say that the province of Nova Scotia had blazed the way and had given the cue to the government of Canada in that respect, and that commission was appointed for the purpose of finding but whether or not the conditions of the country would justify this wide departure of taking the moneys of this Dominion and applying them to technical education. That is my answer to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and I think it is satisfactory. But he, lawyer as he is, will not for a moment question my statement that this road question is entirely within the purview and scope and authority of the local legislatures. The hon. gentleman shakes his head; but I shall 'be thankful if he can find1 one line of authority in the British North America Act giving
us power to devote the moneys of this country to be expended on public roads. There is nothing of the kind. But I am not finding fault with this measure. I am glad the government are taking this [DOT] course, only I wa,nt it done in the proper way. We know that in the province of British Columbia, and some times in the province of Ontario, a great deal of difficulty has been experienced by reason of overlapping authority with regard to the fisheries. In those two provinces it appears that the local governments can issue licenses for fishing purposes, and the Dominion government can issue them also, so that there is always a conflict of authority. The Minister of Railways and Canals, by this Bill, is bringing about a condition which will cause a similar conflict of authority, and if he will follow the course suggested by the right hon. leader of the opposition, he will avoid that. It would appear to me that, as far as any political favouritism is concerned, or favouring one regulation more than another, the chances are that the division 'will be pretty well balanced for many Vears, perhaps always. We have nine local governments, some will he Liberal, some "will be Conservative, probably they will be pretty well balanced at all times.

Do I understand that this measure is, in your opinion, ultra
vires?
1 Mr. McKENZIE. While I am not opposing the measure in any way if I were called on as a lawyer to give an answer on this as a question of law, I would have to say that I do not think that there is any provision in the constitution ^s it stands now which would justify this legislation. If the money thus voted would come as an addition to the subsidies to the provinces and within their control, I would endorse it, but if it is the intention of the government to keep this money under their own control and to work through officers appointed by this government, the Act is going to be a source of inconvenience and very difficult of operation.
In answer to the argument of the Prime Minister that this is analogous to the subsidies granted to railways, I would point but that whereas the subsidy granted to a railway company is hedged in by three Acts of parliament, the Act incorporating a railway company to which the subsidy is granted, the subsidy Act itself, and the general Railway Act, this is not hedged by any Act, it is entirely controlled by the will of the Governor General in Council. That is why we on this side want something in the statute providing that this money shall go to the provinces and shall not be expended according to the caprice of Dominion officers, or of whatever gov-

eminent may be in power here. I think that section 3 of the Act vests the title to this money in the provinces. Once you grant the money to the province, there is only one way that the province is represented and that is by its government, so when you grant the money to the province you vest it in the government of the province and that is the end of it.
What I particularly wish to point out is that what is required on this side is that provincial rights shall be observed. When we are giving this money to any province, we are not giving anything but what is their own. The people of this country are the people just as much in the right of the provinces as in the right of the Dominion; and we must not assume that we are giving gifts to paupers in making these grants. But when we give to the provinces it is our duty to leave it to the provincial authorities to deal with the money. They have the control in dealing with the roads through their representatives in the provincial legislatures and through the provincial government. The only objection I have to this measure is the mode in which it is proposed to carry it out. I am perfectly satisfied that a fair amount of money should be afforded to the different provinces for the purposes of roads, but I hope it will be put absolutely under the control of the different provinces, subject to the supervision by the department. As the Prime Minister said, it was analogous to the railway subsidies. And these subsidies are paid, I understand, on the certificate of an engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals that the railway is finished up to the standard set by certain well defined plans and specifications. All the Minister of Railways need do, if he wishes to keep control of it, is to pay out money to the provinces on the certificate of some officer of the department that the work was properly done according to the standards of the department. Beyond that the expenditures should be entirely under the control of the local government.

I wish to ask the Minister of Railways and Canals whether the appropriation made for each province will be the same year by year. I could see great objections to it if the amount were large one year and small the next. This point has not been touched upon before, so far as I know.
I can give no promise or statement on that; it is a matter of policy.

The hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) accused the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) of displaying partisanship. But it seems to me that the display of partisanship, if there was any, was made by the Mr. McKENZIE.
hon. member for Digby himself. He spoke of the provincial finances of Nova Scotia and mentioned a telegraphic communication from Halifax. As to what he read, I do not think anybody on this side could raise objection to it; but the inference he drew from it is what we object to. He said that the province is perilously near the time when direct taxation is at hand.

If the hon. member will pardon me, I think I said, it would seem from the speech from the Throne that such
was the case.

This bugaboo of direct taxation we have been hearing out in Nova! Scotia for a quarter of a century, and we are no nearer it now than we were twenty-five years ago. The hon. member from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) has well said that the finances of Nova Scotia are, taking everything into consideration, in a very healthy state. What I object to particularly is the insinuation that we on this side are opposed to this legislation and to assisting the provinces in providing improved roads. For myself, sitting on this side of the House, I am in hearty accord with any measure that would improve the condition of the roads in Nova Scotia and elsewhere in Canada. After hearing the discussion, I believe that this Bill, as has been charged, is a very crude Bill. Still, the object of the Bill is a good one-to assist in improving the highways, But when we examine the Bill we find that, stripped of verbiage, it means that this parliament proposes to assist the various provinces by giving them an additional grant for the maintenance and improvement of highways.
Does the hon. gentle-mas disapprove of that?

I do not say I do. But why sail under false colours? Why not put clearly in the enactment what is the effect of the Bill? It does look a.s if there were something behind the motives of the government in bringing in this 'legislation. It is true, they say, that this will implement the promises they made before the election. But the hon. member for Cape Breton and others have pointed out that so far as roads and bridges are concerned, these are entirely within the jurisdiction of the local legislatures. I had the pleasure of being present when the right hon. the Prime Minister received a delegation from Ontario on this subject of improved roads, apd I remembeT distinctly that he stated that the fathers of confederation never expected that this parliament was going to deal with the maintenance of roads and bridges and that we were going very far when we proposed to assist the provinces in the manner we intend to do

this session. It does seem that you do not go very far if this parliament is not going to maintain the rouds after they are built. Reference has been made to trunk roads. I agree with those hon. gentlemen who say that that is not what this country requires; what we want is improvement of the highways that are being used every *day. The great trouble with us in the older provinces is that we have many roads but not enough money to keep up the reads we have.
Will not section 3, cover all that?

I am not referring to any particular section, I am merely referring to the conditions as they obtain in our province. Our roads were not laid out as systematically perhaps as they are in some other provinces, or as they should have been. There is no such regularity about our roads as there is in the western provinces. In Nova Scotia we have a greater mileage according to population than any other province in the Dominion, and we have to bear a Iheavier burden to maintain our Toads than any other province according to population. The discussion this evening has shown that what will suit one province will not suit another. It has been pointed out that in some provinces the municipalities are bearing a certain proportion of the cost of maintaining roads, that in other provinces is borne by the provincial governments, I believe in the province of Ontario the municipality pays t and the Local Legislature 4 of the cost of improving the highways. In certain provinces the municipalities are prepared to bear a certain burden of taxation for the maintenance of roads. But in the province of Nova Scotia we are not. prepared at present to tax the municipalities to the same extent that they are taxed in Ontario, our people have not been educated along those lines. Now in view of these different conditions in the various provinces, is it not better to hand this money over to the provincial legislatures, who can spend it more judiciously for the improvement of roads? The member for Digby (Mr. Jameson), remarked that my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean), had criticised the government because there was no conference provided for between the provinces and the federal government with the view of working out a scheme; he intimated that my hon. friend from Halifax was arguing in favour of delay, and that he was inconsistent in view of the fact that Nova Scotia required more money to enable it to conduct its affairs. But I want to point out that if the member for Digby is sincere in this matter, he will ask the government he supports to pass
this money over to the province so that the roads may be put into good condition at once. The province has all the machinery now, we have engineers as good as; this country can furnish. We have in the road engineer, Mr. McKenzie, as good a road maker as can be found in the whole of Canada. If tire member for Digby is desirous of helping out the province of Nova Scotia and guarding against delay, he will urge the government to pass this money over to the local legislature.
Does the hon. gentleman disagree with the member for Halifax?

I do not. The member for Halifax made no appeal for delay, but he pointed out, what is true, this if this Bill passes now we are going to have delay. If this Bill passes there will be no improvement of the roads inj Nova Scotia or elsewhere next summer; because this legislation provides practically for an agreement with the provinces. Why an agreement with the provinces?' Because it is recognized that under the* British North America Act any man who goes to work on a road in another provi ince would be a trespasser and liable to indictment. If the Minister of Railways sent one of his men down to Nova Scotia to attempt to improve the roads, he could be indicted for interfering with the public highways, unless there was some previous consent obtained from the provincial government.
How does the hon. gentleman expect to make an agreement until he has authority to make it?

I say that the member for Halifax was not arguing for delay in the expenditure, but he was arguing for delay with a view of getting this government and the provincial government together so that everything could be made ready and the machinery could be put into operation for improving the roads as soon as an arrangement had been made.

Does the hon. gentleman think that a delay of a year in passing this legislation would mean an equal delay in the payment of any sum of money which might be made eventually under this legislation to the various provinces?

What difference would it make if the Minister of Railways conferred with the provinces in the month of June, and made an arrangement for working out this scheme, this parliament would not meet again until November, so the Act could not be put into operation until the following year. Now I regard clause 3 also as! rather suspicious. In the marginal note it states that it is a grant of an annual subsidy for highways. I

say the marginal note is misleading, it is not an annual subsidy at all. In the Act itself, it says that the Governor in Council may, in any year, and upon such terms and conditions as are prescribed, grant to any province. It does not say that this grant shall be actually made, it is an appropriation made at such time as suits the Governor in Council. I have no doubt, that in an election year, you will find there will be a grant, but- the year after election there will be no grant.
You ought to know.

It is practical politics, I suppose; but this is too big a matter to be used as a political question. On this side of the House, we think this matter could be better worked out if the money was given to the various provincial legislatures to expend. It is also to be noted in this clause, that the grant may be made to any province; it does not say to the various provinces, but to such province as the Governor in Council may decide. The whole Act seems to have been framed with a view of having more patronage to distribute.
That is exactly what one would conclude from reading the Act. It is true the Act speaks about highways, but the desire is to get the money for election purposes. This is the construction that one would have to put upon the Act from the way in which it is drawn. I do not wish to be taken as criticising the Act. I am strongly in favour of the principle, but I think that the provinces could get far more and the roads would benefit to a much greater extent if a certain amount were apportioned among the provinces either according to mileage of road or population. It is time that there should be an increase in the subsidies to the various provinces. Since 1898 the subsidies to the provinces have been increased twice under the Liberal administration, and I think it is time there [DOT]should be another increase. AfteT 1896 the amount of the subsidy was doubled. I think it was $4,500,000 and it was increased to $9,000,000. Another increase is due and, as my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) said, it is only what the provinces are entitled to.

My hon. friend from Guysborough called the minister's attention to what is unquestionably an omission from section 3 in regard to the question as to whether or not the aid that is proposed to be given by this government shall be extended to bridges. It must be manifest to the minister that it is absurd to talk about improving existing highways or constructing new roads if you are not going to have power to improve old bridges and to- construct new ones. That I need not argue, because I am quite sure that Mr. CHISHOLM (Antdgomsh).
the hon.gentleman will agree with me that the government would have no power to make any expenditure under this Act for the improvement or construction of a bridge as distinct from a highway.
Why not take the bridge to be part of the road?
Sometimes it is not.
My hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) may dispose of it in that easy way.
I am not disposing of It, but as we understand it in our part of the country a bridge is part of the highway.

If the hon. gentleman looks up the legislation in the province of Ontario dealing with the question of roads, he will find that the legislation deals specifically with bridges in addition to roads. There is no such thing as a grant of money to roads without dealing specifically with bridges at the same time.
Certain bridges.
No, not certain bridges.

Up to a certain extent.
Air. A1ACDONALD. Aly hon. friend is mistaken.
In Ontario it is provided that if a bridge exceeds a certain length it is within the jurisdiction of the county council, and in other cases it is under the jurisdiction of the township council.

That is what the minister means. There has been a great deal of discussion as to the general principle of this Bill, and it has been very interesting to hear what hon. gentlemen have had to say with regard to it, but I am free to say that I think a good many of them have taken a great deal for granted in the discussion and in the speeches which they have made. I want to look at this measure in a careful manner, and I submit my hon. friend could not spend money upon bridges unless he put in an amendment which would entitle him to do so.
I think so.

He may have some familiarity with the practice in Ontario but the legislation in other provinces is different. Bridges are one thing and highways are another. They have been dealt with in many provinces of the Dominion as being entirely apart one from the other. Legally they are entirely apart when it comes to a question of liability in regard to the repair of highways. I do not have to go into this question or to make any

very elaborate legal argument about it because in the constituency from which I come there was a leading case on the question of liability for non-repair of a highway-the case of Gerdert vs. Municipality of Pictou county which went to the Privy Council and in which the municipality raised an issue in regard to the maintenance of the highway which had never been raised in any part of the Dominion before. We are here to legislate seriously and if the Minister of Justice, who must take the responsibility for legislation of this character, were here I would go into the question with some *degree of elaboration for the purpose of showing that my hon. friend under this Bill could not deal with bridges either for their improvement or construction unless he includes in the section the words which I propose. My hon. friend surely can take no objection to it. It is extending the principle of his measure and I apprehend that if the proposition is to be a working one, if it is intended that we are going to have anything at all in this measure, we want to get it in such a proposition that can be worked out.
I do not object to putting it in.

I rose for the purpose of suggesting an amendment which I Thought should be accepted.
Mr- COCHRANE. It does not have reference to clause 3.

Yes it has. I propose :
That clause 3 he amended by inserting the words ' or bridges' after the word ' highways ' in the fourth line and the words ' or bridges ' after the word r highways ' in the fifth line and by striking out the words ' both ' in the fifth line and inserting instead the words ' all or any.'

What is the contemplated policy of the government under subsection 3? Does the government contemplate aid to local roads, to trunk roads, or to colonization roads? That is important in deciding as to the merits of the Bill as respects each individual member's vote upon it. If the policy of the government is to use the money for the improvement of local roads, that is a matter of general interest, and I think everybody in the House would vote for it. If it is for the improvement or construction of colonization roads, then certainly those of us who represent the provinces where there is new country to be developed, would, of course, be strongly in favour of that. If, however, the proposal is to expend any large proportion of this money in the establishment of what might be called trunk roads, for the benefit particularly of the automobile section of the population, I am not so sure that
every member of this House would be pre pared to strongly support the measure. It is important that the minister should give us some information as to what policy the government has in mind.

This will be largely a matter of policy to be determined on between the local governments and the federal government. I would hope, in dealing with the different provincial governments, to lay down a policy that could be worked to from year to year, so that we would not have checker-board improvements. In my opinion the scheme will he largely worked out in connection with the local governments of the different provinces, probably one province might prefer one scheme and another province another.

I do not think that is any explanation at all. The Bill is couched in very general terms, and that being so, it is only fair that the members should know what policy the government proposes to pursue. Of course, if the minister says the Federal government is going to pursue any policy that will suit any of the provincial governments that would be quite intelligible.

Probably the roads in the provinces represented by my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) would require different treatment from the roads in Ontario or Quebec, and I have had no hesitation in saying from the very beginning that we would work in connection with the local governments.

If it is understood that what is done will be on the responsibility of the local governments, then we can understand where we are, and I would be willing to accept that position, but if the Federal government is going to exercise jurisdiction in the distribujiion of the money it is only fair the minister should gajf what particular class of roads he proposes most to favour.

I did not propose speaking on this question, but the hon. gentleman from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), in reply to what I thought was a respectful question, took occasion to make a personal reference to me. I asked him if he thought there would be any danger under the arrangement proposed, of the money advanced by the Dominion government to the provincial government of Nova Scotia, being garnisheed by creditors of the provincial government, and, for want of a better answer, the hon. member stated that perhaps I had in my own experience, suffered from the garnishee laws of my province. Now, I do not pose as a millionaire; I am not wealthy at all; I am not in the fortunate position of some gentlemen opposite in that I have not received offices

of emolument from the government, and I have not had an opportunity of laying by money in that way. I have not fed extensively on the public treasury nor do I expect to do so, and consequently, I am not a millionaire, but my assets have never been garnisheed, and I never expect that they will be. I want to say that if I had been as prodigal with the expenditure of my income as the province of Nova Scotia has been, I would expect such a procedure. I want to say further that in the carrying out of the provisions of this Bill, I hope the minister will exercise a great deal of care, in respect to the province of Nova Scotia. Hon. gentlemen opposite who come from Nova Scotia have advocated that the money be paid over directly to the province and that the Dominion authorities part with any control over its expenditure. Well, judging from the history of the Nova Scotia government in the past, with regard to road construction, that would be a most dangerous policy to follow. Several years ago the province of Nova Scotia borrowed some $600,000 for the purpose of constructing permanent roads, and they used this money, not to make roads, but to make votes, and to-day there is not a foot of permanent highway in that province.
Is that the policy you propose adopting now?

That is a policy I do not propose adopting. I advocate that the Dominion government working in conjunction with the provincial government, should be thoroughly satisfied that every dollar is being expended in making roads and not in making votes. These gentlemen opposite do not seem to have any conception of making roads; their idea in reference to the Road Act is something to make votes with for themselves, and consequently you see them divided as to how this' money shall be expended. The hon. member from Welland (Mr. German) says: Don't give this money to the provincial government. And why?
Because the government of Ontario is Conservative he says, give it to the municipalities. The hon. member for Halifax, the hon. member for Antigonish, and the illustrious member from North Cape Breton say, give this money to the provincial governments, because they know that the provincial government in the province of Nova Scotia is in a very difficult corner, and they want this money to be expended to make votes for themselves in the coming elections. My hon. friend from North Cape Breton represents a constituency in which there was a good deal of jobbery in connection with the expenditure of the $600,000 to which I referred, and he should be the last man on earth to advocate giving the provincial government a free hand in"the expenditure of this money. I sin-

cerely hope that nothing of the kind will be done. A few years ago the federal subsidy to the province of Nova Scotia was materially increased. It was hoped by some admirers of the provincial government that it would use those funds for constructing highways; but instead of doing that, they used it to increase their own salaries and appoint certain zealous officials. I venerate to a large degree the hon. member for Halifax, and on most matters would be inclined to take his opinion, but I cannot but remember that he sat for some years in the provincial government of Nova Scotia, and if he had any knowledge of roads he did not show it then, and I do not think he is in a position to instruct this House on that subject.

There is no one in this House who is more willing to give a respectful reply to a respectful question than myself. I would be the last man in this House to give any other than the most respectful reply to the hon. member for Annapolis if he had asked a respectful question; but I leave it to the judgment of any hon. member whether it was a serious or respectful question to ask a representative of the fair province of Nova Scotia if I did not think it was a dangerous thing to pay money over to the credit of that province for fear it might be garnisheed. There is an old saying and a true one that it is an ill bird that befouls its own nest. Let the hon. member for Annapolis think what a reflection he has put upon the province that has given three premiers to this Dominion. The province of Nova Scotia is proud of having given to this Dominion the present Premier. Yet the hon. member for Annapolis stands up in this House and says seriously that the financial condition of that province is such that any moneys paid to its credit are liable to be garnisheed. I want the province of Nova Scotia to know that that is the reputation which the hon. member wishes to give to the province of Nova Scotia in the presence of this House. Every province of this Dominion has been represented in this discussion, but not a man has said anything disrespectful of the credit and standing of his own province except the hon. member for Annapolis. I want the good people of Annapolis to know that they have sent a gentleman here who thinks it his duty to speak in such a disrespectful manner' of the fair province of Nova Scotia. The hon. member says there was jobbery in my county. I do not know to what county he Tefers.
Victoria.

I defy him to produce the record to show that there is a word of truth in that statement. It would not be parliamentary to say that the hon. gentle-

man uttered a falsehood, but I do say that he was born with a predisposition to strike the truth at an impossible angle.

The hon. gentleman is very bold in challenging me to produce records that are about a thousand miles away. He knows very well about the circumstances. He says that I spoke against the reputation of the province of Nova Scotia. He must know that that is incorrect. I never said a word against the reputation of the province of Nova Scotia, and I want to say, in justice to the reputation of my province, that the good people of the province intend at the very earliest opportunity to put out of office the men who have put the province in debt and have given it nothing but bad government.

Clause 3 of the Bill provides that the Governor in Council may in any year grant to any province in aid of improvement of highways; that is, it may grant to any one province and leave out all the others. The language bears that construction, at all events. I do not think we should allow the clause to pass id that shape. I think we should assert the right of each province to participate in any grant that is made. I know that the Prime Minister has stated that he will observe that principle in the distribution of the money that is proposed to be spent under this Act. The Minister of Railways has also made the statement that the money will be expended according to the population of the various provinces, but they will not be here forever, and my objection to the clause is that it does not express that idea. As it reads, it simply gives the government power by order in council to grant money to any one province. Therefore, I beg to move that the following be added to clause 3:
Provided always that when any such grant is made to any one province each of the other provinces shall be entitled to a proportional grant based on the population of such province.
I desire to second this resolution.
Lost.

My hon. friends are calling ' lost ' as if this discussion had been carried on altogether by hon. gentlemen on this side. Quite as many have spoken on the government side as on this side, and there is no desire on the part of the opposition to obstruct or delay this Bill. What objection can there be to putting in the Bill what the Prime Minister to-day said was the policy of the government. It would not be fair for the government to say that in one year all the grant would go to one province. That is surely not the intention of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The adoption of the amendment proposed would render the Bill useless and abortive. The Bill is based on the idea that the money is to he spent by arrangement with provincial governments so that if we adopted this amendment, then if the government failed to come to an agreement with Nova Scotia, for instance, no money could be spent in New Brunswick or any other province because of this amendment.
There is nothing in section 3 in regard to agreement with the provinces,that is fixed by subsequent sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not see that it would make any difference whether that is fixed by section 3 or a subsequent section.
We are not saying you must spend money in the province, but, that you must appropriate a similar sum.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Which means that unless you make an arrangement with every province the whole scheme will fail. The matter may be safely left to the good sense of the government and to the good judgment of the people who would not tolerate any injustice as between the provinces.

The minister's argument is erroneous as a matter of law and of interpretation of this Bill. There is not a line in section 3 which makes the voting of the money contingent upon the making of an arrangement with a province. Sections 4 and 5 control section 3 and limit the power of the government and prevent them making an expenditure except under the conditions contained in the agreement arrived at with the provincial governments.

When the Bill was introduced some days ago the minister stated that the money which was to be appropriated every year should be apportioned among the different provinces as the subsidies are now apportioned. The object would be to work in with the different local governments. In order to make the intention surer, I said:
I was asking the hon. gentleman to tell us if there was any basis of allotment among the provinces. The provincial subsidy is based on population.

Yes, I explained it was to be on the same basis as that upon which the subsidies are granted to the provinces.
When the Bill was distributed 'and I came to read it I found no such disposition in it.
Therefore, in order to make the matter certain, I moved an amendment to insert this in the Bill. But the Prime Minister said there was no necessity for that, because the Minister of Railways in intro-

ducing the Bill, had told us that such was the intention, and upon this he asked the House to vote down the amendment, I supposed then that matter would be disposed of in Committee of the Whole, and that words would toe inserted to carry out what was declared to be the intention of the law. But that has not been done. Surely, so important a matter is not to be left simply to the good-will of the -government. As I have said, governments do not live forever and a succeeding government may not agree with the disposal of money in such a case as this proposed by the government it replaces. And even the same government will sometimes change its mind. So, if it is the intention of the government that this money is to be divided among the provinces according to proposal, surely that should be incorporated in the Bill. The amendment of my hon. friend, I think, does not convey the idea. Therefore, I move, in amendment to the amendment, that the following words toe inserted as subsection 2 of section 3:
The sums of money voted in any year to be expended under this Act shall be apportioned among, the different provinces of the Dominion according to the population of said provinces as established by the last census for the time being. *
Lost.

Before that vote is taken, ' it is surely due to the committee that the government should state why they decline to implement the policy stated on the introduction of this measure and on the second reading. We have discussed this measure assuming that at the proper time the government would express their policy in the Bill. Why is it not done? Hon. gentlemen opposite are saying ' lost,' but there is no explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) heard the right hon. leader of the government this afternoon make a clear and distinct statement that when parliament was being asked to vote this money the money would be appropriated an amount for each province in Canada, and there is no purpose to be served by the amendment of the right hon. leader of the opposition. The motion was rejected this afternoon, and I am sure it will be rejected again to-night.

That is not the intention as explained by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen). He just intimated to the committee that an agreement could be made regarding one province only, and an appropriation made for it while the rest of the provinces would be left out.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, no.
What, then, is the contention of the hon. minister?
Lost.

Hon. gentlemen opposite say ' lost.' But we want to know why this amendment should be rejected. That is all we ask. We propose that the money be distributed according to population. The Prime Minister has said that it is the intention to do so. We want that put in black and white in the law. And not1 only is that refused, but we are refused an explanation.
Question.

Surely a proposition of this kind, a serious proposition, and one involving a new departure is not going to be disposed of in this fashion. Hon. members opposite cannot complain of captious discussion on the part of the opposition.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen who have been here all evening know that more members spoke on the government side than on this side. And they spoke at length. They lauded the government for this Bill. One hon, gentleman wanted to see a great ieaeral highway from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Others on the same side opposed that, and propounded all kinds of theories as to how this money should be spent. After listening for three hours to a discussion of these academic problems, we come to the details of the Bill. We ask the government to incorporate in the measure the statement made by the Minister of Railways in introducing it and by the Prime Minister on the second reading. And the only answer we get is the cry of ' lost.' That is not a dignified way to deal with a grgat question, and one in which this parliament is entering for the first time upon an expenditure of road money, dealing with a matter which seems to trench upon the sphere of the provincial authority. And we have this anomaly that while the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers), is the third minister to state that the government is to divide this money among the provinces, according to population, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), tells us that that is not the policy.
Oh, oh.

On the contrary the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hazen) argued against the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) by telling him that it would have this effect, that, if the government should

vote money for expenditure in any particular province, having made an agreement with that province, the amendment would compel them to vote money for expenditure in other provinces where they had no agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald), must know that he has misconstrued me, or, I should say that it is evident that the hon. gentleman has misunderstood me, and I am sorry I did not make myself clear. I said that the effect of the amendment of the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair)-which by the way, was not accepted by the leader of the opposition
It was an improvement.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: -the effect would be that if the government made an agreement with the government of one province for an expenditure of a certain sum in that province and failed to make an arrangement with some other province, they would be precluded from spending money in any province; just the reverse of the position stated by my hon. friend from Pictou.

I am glad the minister has succeeded in getting himself into a position which, he thinks, in some degree consistent with that taken by the other ministers.
My hon. friend has reaffirmed his attitude. The committee has not forgotten the discussion we had a few moments ago in regard to that matter, when I showed him that the amendment of the member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) would not have the effect which he anticipated. Do I understand the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to say now that it is the policy of the government, when *hey take a vote in any one year, to take a vote for all the provinces at the same time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the policy laid down by the Prime Minister, to which I adhere.

I think that was the policy of the government as stated by the Prime Minister this afternoon, and as stated now by the Minister of Railways and Canals, but the hon. gentlemen opposite who are responsible for carrying out this Bill will not put it in the law. The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) seems to be the boss of this administration. He stated-I remember his words very well -after the Prime Minister spoke and said that was the intention of the government, the member for Simcoe made a general demurrer. Oh no, he sarys, I don't think that is the proper principle, to expend this money according to population, there are some localities that should have more than 118
others. That was the view taken by the hon. member for Simcoe, and he is the real master of the administration. Now, the government will not put into the law what the Prime Minister declared was his intention this afternoon, because the member for Simcoe objects to it. I congratulate my hon. friend on his power over the present administration.
Amendment to the amendment (Mr. Sinclair) negatived.
Amendment (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) negatived.
It is time to adjourn now.	[DOT]
No, finish it up, it won't take us. long.
You cannot do it. It is not fair at one o'clock in the morning to ask us to sit here ajny longer.
I move that the committee rise and report progress.

Motion agreed to.
Mr. COCHRANE moved the adjournment of the House.
Will we take up the same thing on Monday?
No, the Grain Bill will be up on Monday, and other government Bills, and then estimates of the Department of the Interior.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.58 a.m. Saturday.
Monday, February 26, 1912.
